chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Every position is measured against one test: is it constitutional, and does it serve the people? Where a change requires the legislature, this page says so. Share the plan X Facebook LinkedIn Email Copy link Amendment 1: mandatory budget stabilization transfers # Florida should carry a strong reserve, and the state has built one. The legislature can already fund the reserve, and does. No amendment is needed. A fixed dollar formula in the constitution makes a budgeting choice permanent. It moves spending decisions out of the public appropriations process, where you can watch them. Constitutions set limits on power. They are not the place for accounting rules.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Ends property tax on farm equipment and tangible personal property used in agricultural production, starting 2027. Taxing a tractor like inventory pushes cost onto growers already squeezed by disease, imports, and land prices. Estimated revenue effect is roughly $31 million in year one. Small against the state budget, meaningful to a family operation. I support it (my property tax cut policies go further) with one reservation stated plainly. Raises the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Cuts the non-homestead assessment cap from 10 percent to 5 percent. This moves in the direction I have argued for: protect the home you live in.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: The reservation: the full break goes immediately only to people who were Florida residents by December 31, 2026. Later arrivals wait five years. The text itself hedges with "to the extent permitted by the U.S. Constitution." The drafters know that provision is vulnerable under the right to travel. If that provision is struck, the rest should stand. Local governments project significant revenue loss by 2031. That is the replacement-math problem anyone proposing property tax relief owes you. I will stand up a public replacement commission and publish county-by-county numbers. Share this section X Facebook LinkedIn Email Copy link

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Florida homeowners pay the highest property insurance premiums in the country. The reasons sit inside filings almost nobody reads. The state's own consultant found an accounting scheme where profits are hidden in affiliates while insurance companies claim losses. Up to 63% of premiums were affiliate fees. Direct the Office of Insurance Regulation to publish loss ratios, reinsurance costs, executive pay, and rate justifications in plain language. Require whole-company accounting so no carrier declares a loss while its affiliates book the profit. Cap insurer profit as a share of revenue minus expenditures, and return surplus back to policyholders.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Build any cap with actuarial review and solvency protection so carriers stay and pay claims. Expand My Safe Florida Home and tie it to enforced building codes. Make mitigation discounts real and visible on the bill. A policy is a contract. A homeowner who is wrongly denied must be able to enforce it. Restore the policyholder's right to sue a carrier that denies, underpays, or slow-walks a covered claim. Restore one-way attorney fee recovery for a policyholder who wins. Without it, a $40,000 roof claim is not worth litigating and carriers know it. The 2022 and 2023 changes were sold as ending frivolous litigation. What they ended was the leverage an ordinary homeowner had.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Keep real sanctions for genuinely fraudulent claims and for contractors who inflate them. Fraud enforcement and a homeowner's right to sue are not in tension. Citizens is the state-backed insurer of last resort. If Citizens cannot pay claims after a major storm, Florida law allows assessments on policyholders statewide, including people who are not Citizens customers. That is a tax that appears on your bill without a vote. Require every Florida policy to state the assessment exposure in plain language. Before any takeout offer reaches a policyholder, publish the financial condition of the carrier making it, including affiliate structure and claims-payment record.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Let policyholders decline a takeout without penalty. No takeout approvals for carriers that fail solvency screening. Keep Citizens rates actuarially sound. The glide path should not outrun Florida wages. Floridians pay among the highest auto rates in the country. Apply the same whole-company accounting standard used for property carriers. Telematics. The rule is consent and ownership: Ban manufacturer-installed telematics that transmit driving or location data without the owner's express consent. A car you bought should not report on you by default. If a driver chooses an insurance telematics device, that is their call.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: The insurer may collect only what is necessary to price that policy. Nothing more. The driver owns the data and can see everything held on them. The driver can delete it at any time without losing coverage. Require honest disclosure to buyers and renters before they sign. Open the market to private alternatives. Address inland flooding and repetitive-loss properties. The risk does not stop at the coast. The federal program most Floridians actually use: Most flood policies in Florida are written through the National Flood Insurance Program, and its risk-rating overhaul moved a lot of premiums sharply upward.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Congress has run the program on short-term extensions for years. Every lapse freezes closings in a state where people are trying to buy and sell homes. A governor does not set NFIP rates. Here is what Florida can do, and I will do all of it. Fund elevation, flood-proofing, and drainage mitigation directly. Mitigation is the only thing that lowers a premium permanently, and it lowers what the state pays to rebuild. Get every eligible community into the Community Rating System. Those discounts come off residents' premiums for work local governments are largely doing anyway.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Honest, current flood maps, and full flood history disclosed to every buyer and renter before they sign. People should know what they are buying. Open the private flood market as real competition rather than a last resort. Press for a long-term reauthorization and an affordability glide path tied to what a household can pay, not only to what the model says the risk is. Preparedness and insurance are the same problem. A hardened home is cheaper to insure and cheaper to rebuild. Pre-position supplies and ready county resilience centers before the cone appears. Fully fund the Division of Emergency Management. Build a state disaster reserve so Florida can respond without waiting on FEMA.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Every hurricane recovery contract public: the vendor, the scope, the price, the change orders, and who approved them. Posted as they are signed, not released after the season when nobody is looking. Debris hauling measured and verified before payment. Volume fraud after a storm is the oldest trick in the business. Fraud is prosecuted as fraud. Charges, prison, restitution. Permanent debarment from state and local work for the company and for the people who ran it, so the same crew does not reappear under a new name next storm. Pre-qualified vendor lists built before the season, with rates set in advance, so the state is not negotiating at a premium while people are under water.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Share this section X Facebook LinkedIn Email Copy link Housing costs and who is buying our homes # Institutional investors are buying single-family homes and renting them back to the people who used to be able to buy them. A family bidding on a first house should not be bidding against a fund.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Under federal law, any for-profit entity or corporation that controls 350 or more single-family homes nationwide is restricted from buying additional existing single-family properties. In Florida I will make that zero. Single family homes are for families, not corporations . Families who own a second home or investors who buy a home to rehab it and put it back on the market will be exempt. Properties built for renting, such as apartment complexes, are also exempt. Bar institutional investors from buying single-family homes in Florida. Exempt legitimate builders, community land trusts, nonprofits, and small local landlords.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Renter protections: just-cause eviction, capped security deposits, 90 days notice before a rent increase above 5 percent. No mass sprawl. Walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods where people live near where they work. Require community approval for large developments, not a rubber stamp. Direct federal housing money to community land trusts, nonprofits, local builders, and veterans housing, with public transparency on every dollar. Money that ends up with large developers and institutional investors does not solve affordability. You should not lose a home you already paid for because you cannot cover the tax on it.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Full elimination takes a constitutional amendment and 60 percent voter approval. That is your decision, not a governor's. Beyond Amendment 3, my position is targeted: Eliminate property taxes on homesteaded homes within 200 percent of the county median. For example, if the median home price in your county is $300k and your home is worth $600k (2x the median) or less - no property taxes. Non-homesteaded property and second homes do not qualify. This protects primary residences, not portfolios. Police, fire, schools, and rural counties with thin commercial tax bases depend on that revenue. A public replacement commission will publish county-by-county numbers before a vote.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Owners face six-figure assessments while trying to read board finances they were never shown. Enforce structural reserve and milestone inspection rules. Require transparency on board finances and management contracts. Create state-backed low-interest loans for mandatory repairs. The requirements adopted after Surfside should not be quietly weakened because compliance became inconvenient. Require CDD bond disclosure before purchase. Protection from sudden lot rent increases for residents who own the home but rent the land. Protection from displacement when a park is sold. Protections for seniors on fixed incomes. Child care costs more than in-state college tuition for many Florida families.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: The state treats an affordability problem as a private one. Fully fund VPK at a rate that reflects what care actually costs. Address child care worker pay, which is why seats sit empty while waitlists grow. Create incentives for employer-supported care. Publish provider capacity and waitlists by county. Extend voucher program to younger children, and create subsidy programs for mothers to raise their young children Suspend state gas taxes during price spikes. Negotiate bulk fuel contracts for the state. My goal is to end tolls for Florida residents. Full audit of toll road revenue and complete transparency on SunPass.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Where the bonds on a road are retired, the toll comes off. That is not a goal, it is the deal taxpayers were given. Where bond covenants still govern, the state honors the contract. I will say so rather than promise something I cannot deliver. Publish every road's bond status, payoff date, and annual revenue so Floridians can see which tolls are still owed and which are habit. Resident exemption first, funded by the roads that are already paid off, then expanded as bonds retire. Support distributed solar and battery storage. Back Florida solar manufacturers and installers. Utilities should not convert the energy transition into a monopoly they bill you for.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Rates are set by the Public Service Commission, so a governor's leverage is appointments and legislation. Florida builds roads and calls it a transportation plan. Adding lanes buys a few years, then the congestion returns. Publish cost per mile on every major project, before and after completion. Fund real alternatives in the corridors that need them: I-4, Tampa Bay, South Florida. Commuters stuck in traffic pay for the absence of a choice with their time and their fuel. On passenger rail: publish incident data by crossing, fund grade separation and crossing safety where deaths are concentrated, and hold operators to it.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: I oppose confiscating e-bikes. Several Florida cities have moved toward seizures and outright age bans. Taking a kid's bike is not a safety program. Riders under 18: helmet and required safety equipment, lights after dark, and the same rules of the road everyone else follows. Enforce the riding, not the ownership. A citation to the rider or the parent, not a seized bike. Stunting and trick riding belong off public streets. Fund bike parks and skate parks so there is somewhere to do it legally. One statewide framework rather than a different rule in every city, so a family crossing a line on a Saturday is not suddenly breaking the law.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Florida caps interest at 18 and 25 percent under Chapter 687. Federally chartered banks are exempt under the National Bank Act, which is why a Floridian can hold a card charging far more than Florida law allows. Regulate state-chartered lenders aggressively. Cap payday and title loans at the state limit. Create a Florida consumer financial protection office. Require plain-language total-cost disclosure before signing. Press the congressional delegation on the rate-export loophole. Examine conditioning the right to do business here on compliance with Florida usury standards, and litigate it if necessary.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Florida has had no state personal income tax since 1924 and it is written into our constitution. I will defend that prohibition. I oppose federal income tax on labor. A governor cannot repeal it. A governor can build a coalition of the states that already refuse to tax income and put sustained pressure on Washington. I intend to lead that coalition. Keep reducing state debt and growing the surplus. Remove state investments from foreign entities. Florida takes in a great deal of revenue. The problem is not that the state is poor. It is that too much of what comes in leaks out before it does anything for you.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Rigorous independent audits of all 67 counties, on a published schedule, with the findings public. The same standard applied to every state agency and every entity spending state money, including contractors and quasi-public authorities. Fraud and misappropriation of public funds prosecuted as crimes, not resolved with a repayment and a letter. Debarment from future state work for any vendor or official found to have defrauded the public. A public spending dashboard down to the contract level, so waste is visible to anyone who wants to look rather than only to an auditor.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: A royalty on bulk water extracted for commercial resale. Right now a bottler pays a permit fee and sells a public resource back to the people who own it. Energy. A state with this much sun exports none of it and imports nearly all the hardware. Agriculture and food production, rebuilt rather than managed into decline. Tourism growth, and tourist development revenue spent on the infrastructure that sustains it. New industries that export goods and services out of Florida instead of recirculating the same dollars. A visitor surcharge, with the math shown:

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Florida hosted 143.3 million visitors in 2025. They use the roads, the beaches, the water, the emergency rooms, and the hurricane response that residents pay for. A flat $4 surcharge on visitor transactions, paid almost entirely by people who do not live here. Hotel and motel room nights about 100 million about $400 million Vacation rental nights about 35 million about $140 million Rental car days 90 to 110 million $360 to $440 million Total, lodging and rental cars about $900 million to $1 billion Florida already collects a $2.00 per day rental car surcharge, so that line is not a guess. It is a rate change on a tax the state already administers.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Lodging already collects the tourist development tax, so the mechanism exists and costs nothing new to run. Air travel is not on this list. Federal law bars states from taxing passengers in air commerce, and the fee on your ticket is a federally authorized airport charge, not a state tax. Anyone promising you revenue from that has not read the statute. Cruise is not on this list either. The Tonnage Clause limits what a state may charge a vessel, and the ports already levy their own per-passenger fees. That route runs through the ports, not Tallahassee.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Dedicated by law to the things visitors use: coastal and water infrastructure, emergency response, and the roads carrying the traffic. Not to the general fund, where it would disappear. About a billion dollars a year is real money and it funds a great deal of what is on this page. It does not replace tolls, and it does not come close to replacing homestead property tax. Anyone who tells you one surcharge covers those is doing arithmetic they have not shown you.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Gaming revenue is in the same category. The Seminole compact is projected at roughly $4.4 billion through fiscal 2028-29, rising toward about $890 million a year. That money is already in the budget. It is not sitting unused waiting to be assigned. Every tax reduction on this page comes with published replacement math before it takes effect, not after. No new program without a funding source named in the same breath. Keep reducing state debt and growing the reserve. A state that spends its surplus in good years has nothing when a storm takes a county apart. Share this section X Facebook LinkedIn Email Copy link Roughly 800,000 Floridians fall into the coverage gap.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Direct the Agency for Health Care Administration to pursue a waiver. Durable funding requires the legislature. Florida's prescription drug importation program is signed into law and federally approved but stalled. Press to start bulk purchasing. Florida has more people on the ACA marketplace than any other state. I support extending the enhanced credits as a bridge rather than letting premiums jump overnight. But subsidies paid to insurers without price transparency feed the system that drove costs up. The real fix is lowering what care costs: importation, price transparency, disclosure of pharmaceutical financial ties, and closing the coverage gap.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Florida has a nursing shortage, a mental health access shortage, and a substance abuse treatment capacity shortage at the same time. Burnout is pushing people out of the field faster than we replace them. This is a standalone statewide problem and I will treat it as one. Florida is receiving a large multi-year settlement from opioid manufacturers and distributors. That money was paid because people died. Publish every dollar: what came in, where it went, what it bought, by county. Spend it on treatment capacity, recovery housing, and overdose prevention. No backfilling budgets that were already committed. Independent oversight with public reporting, not an agency grading its own work.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Share this section X Facebook LinkedIn Email Copy link Florida's $15 minimum took effect September 30, 2026 under the amendment voters approved. Tie future increases to Florida's cost of living rather than a national index. Remove the preemption that blocks local governments from setting their own wage floors. At a certain wage level, corporations automate. Wage policy alone leaves people stranded. Florida should be building entrepreneurs, skilled tradesmen, and craftsmen, not a permanent minimum-wage workforce. Real investment in vocational programs, apprenticeships, and agricultural training alongside any wage floor.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Gig workers deserve injury coverage and transparent pay calculations without being misclassified into a category that serves the platform instead of the worker. Occupational licensing reform to reduce barriers to work. Streamlined recognition of military credentials. Support maritime and fishing industries and protect independent commercial fishermen. Tourism is Florida's largest industry and one of its largest employers. The people who staff it frequently cannot afford to live near the places they work. Tourist development tax revenue should fund infrastructure, workforce housing, and beach and water quality work in the counties that generate it, not stadium subsidies.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Publish a full audit of state tourism marketing spending, including contracts and performance. A public agency spending public money on advertising should show what it bought. Workforce housing near resort and service corridors, starting with the Keys and the coastal counties where the problem is most acute. Florida's economy runs on tourism, agriculture, construction, and retirees. Three of those are exposed to a bad storm season and the fourth to a bad market. The answer is not a tax break for whoever shows up. It is building industries on what Florida already has. Solar manufacturing and installation. We have the sun, the roofs, and the demand, and we import nearly all of the hardware.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Housing technology: materials and construction science aimed at building storm-resistant housing faster and cheaper. Florida is the country's hardest test case and should be its laboratory. Food and agricultural science, starting with citrus greening and extending to heat-tolerant crops and water-efficient growing. Water technology. A state with our aquifer problems should be exporting the solutions. Agritourism and direct-to-consumer agriculture as income that keeps working land in production. Research funding at Florida institutions tied to getting results into Florida businesses. Procurement preference for Florida-made where price and capability are comparable.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Apprenticeships and technical programs aimed at these industries specifically. No subsidies to out-of-state companies for relocating a headquarters and little else. Rural Florida, and a fair amount of inland Florida, still cannot get reliable service. That holds back farms, small businesses, telehealth, and schoolwork. Take federal broadband money whenever it comes without conditions that trade away state authority. Read what is attached before signing, and say publicly what the terms are. Spend it on reaching unserved addresses, not on upgrading places that already have service. Publish the map of who is covered, who is not, and which provider took money to fix it.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Florida should be the easiest state in the country to build a digital asset business in, and the hardest state in which to have your own property taken from you. Holding your own keys is holding your own property. No Florida law will restrict self-custody, require a third-party custodian, or treat a private wallet as a regulated entity. No state central bank digital currency, and no state recognition of one as money. Seizure of digital assets follows the same rule as everything else on this page: conviction first, warrant always, and the same bar as seizing a car or a bank account. Chapter 560 was written for wire transfer businesses and is being applied to things it was never drafted for.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Writing software is not money transmission. Running a node, publishing code, validating transactions, and building non-custodial tools do not make you a money transmitter. A clear line: if you hold someone else's funds, you are licensed and audited. If you never touch customer funds, you are a software company. Published guidance and a real answer within a fixed timeframe, so a builder knows where they stand before they hire anyone. Accept digital assets for state fees, taxes, and permits. Florida may hold bitcoin and ether directly , not only convert them on receipt.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Bounded and published: a cap stated as a share of the portfolio, named custody arrangements, and never money needed to operate in the next budget cycle. The eligibility standard is written by asset characteristics, depth of market, settlement history, and auditable custody, rather than by naming tickers in statute. Today bitcoin and ether are what meets it, and the standard will not need a new bill every time the market moves. Quarterly public reporting of holdings, cost basis, and current value. Public money, public ledger. No leverage, no lending, no yield products with state funds. This is a reserve, not a trading desk.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Public ledgers for public records where they add verifiable transparency, starting with procurement and contract histories. A Florida business may accept, hold, and pay in bitcoin or ether without a separate state license for doing so. No state agency may deny a license, permit, or charter to a lawful business because it deals in digital assets. The state will not pressure a bank to drop a customer over a lawful digital asset business. Contracts denominated in or settled with digital assets are enforceable in Florida courts, with the same rules of construction as any other contract.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: I said data centers pay their full costs for water, energy, waste heat, and grid impact. Mining operations are data centers and the same rule applies to them. No discriminatory zoning or punitive utility rates aimed at mining, and no subsidized rates either. The same rate card as any other industrial customer. Residential ratepayers do not subsidize anyone's electricity, whatever the business is. That is the deal: no special burden, no special favor. Share this section X Facebook LinkedIn Email Copy link Agencies that serve the public, not the industry #

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: An agency built to regulate an industry ends up staffed by people from that industry, writing rules that industry can live with, then hiring those people back. That is how the insurance office, the utility commission, and the water districts stopped working for you. Tighten lobbying rules, revolving-door restrictions, and gift rules. Publish agency performance scorecards so service delivery is measured in public. The order matters: the people, then the Constitution, then government, then the people who work in it. Agents of the government sit at the bottom of that list, not the top. Every change to a software codebase is recorded: what changed, who changed it, when.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Legislation has no such record, which is why language nobody claims authorship of appears in a bill at two in the morning. Require public version history for every bill, showing every change, every author, and every outside party who influenced the text. If a lobbyist wrote the paragraph, your name should be on the paragraph. No other candidate in this race is proposing this. Florida's public records law is one of the strongest in the country on paper. It has been weakened by hundreds of statutory exemptions added one at a time. It has been weakened further by agencies that comply slowly enough to make a request pointless.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Audit every exemption and publish the list with its original justification. Sunset exemptions so each one has to be defended again rather than accumulating forever. Publish agency response times for records requests. Penalties for unreasonable delay should fall on the agency, not the requester. Authority belongs at the lowest level of government competent to exercise it. Tallahassee has spent years overriding counties and cities on wages, housing, land use, and more. A statewide standard is sometimes right. When the state preempts a local decision, it should have to identify the specific statewide interest that justifies it.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Blanket preemption with no stated reason is not federalism, it is convenience. I oppose preemption that strips local governments of the ability to respond to local conditions, starting with the wage preemption in Section 218.077. A governor fills judicial vacancies through the judicial nominating commissions and appoints the commissioners. Publish every applicant, every interview, and every commissioner's vote. Appoint on qualification, record, and judicial temperament. No political litmus tests in either direction. A judge's job is to apply the law as written, including when it produces a result the governor does not like.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: A judge appointed by the governor, or whose appointment is pending before him, does not sit on a case involving that governor's administration. Recusal is not a favor to the parties. It is what makes the ruling worth anything. I will not appoint anyone who treats a seat on the bench as a continuation of their political career. Follow the law. That is the whole position. Money recovered in a state Medicaid settlement is public money. Where it went, who directed it, and under what authority are questions with documents behind them. Legislative subpoenas should be answered, not negotiated down.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: A charitable foundation operating inside a state agency invites exactly this. Either it is a state program subject to public records and audit, or it is a private charity with no access to state settlement money. It cannot be both. No official, elected or appointed, is above the audit. That includes a governor, and it would include me. Public Service Commission appointments # The PSC sets what you pay for electricity and water. A governor's real leverage over utility rates is who sits on it, so that is where the reform has to be.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Demonstrated competence in engineering, utility economics, accounting, or consumer law. This is a technical job and it should be held by people who can read a rate filing. No one who has worked for or lobbied on behalf of a regulated utility in the previous four years. At least one seat reserved for a commissioner with a consumer advocacy background. Applications, résumés, and conflict disclosures published when submitted. Public interviews, livestreamed and archived. A nominating council that is not controlled by people who take utility campaign money, with the conflicts of every member published.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Every contact between a commissioner and a utility logged and published, including the date, the participants, and the subject. Four-year ban on going to work for a utility the commissioner regulated, with real penalties rather than an honor system. Fund the Office of Public Counsel so ratepayers have representation comparable to what the utilities bring. Rate orders written in plain language explaining what changed and why. No voting machines running proprietary code the public cannot inspect. An election system nobody is allowed to examine is asking for trust it has not earned. This is a systems question before it is a partisan one. No foreign influence over Florida policy #

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: No foreign government should have influence over Florida policy. The standard is neutral and applies to all of them: Russian, Israeli, Chinese, or any other. Prohibit state contracts with foreign-government-owned or controlled companies. Work with the Cabinet to keep state pension funds out of foreign entities engaged in human rights violations. The State Board of Administration is governed by the governor, the Chief Financial Officer, and the Attorney General together, so that one is a shared decision. No special treatment for any race, religion, or nationality. That is the principle, and it runs in both directions.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: No Floridian gets more or less protection under state law because of who they are. No foreign government gets a carve-out in Florida statute because of which one it is. A rule that can only be stated by naming one country or one community is not a rule. It is a favor. Where Florida law currently singles out one nation or one group, I will move it to a neutral standard that covers everyone. Florida's scrutinized-companies framework from 2016, and its 2025 expansion to schools, nonprofits, local governments, and grant applicants, condition public contracts and investment on a political position about a foreign government.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Courts in several states have enjoined comparable laws as compelled speech and as unconstitutional conditions. I will move to repeal them. A Florida business should win or lose a contract on price, capability, and performance. This follows directly from the First Amendment position above. A speech condition I like today is a speech condition pointed at me tomorrow. Threats, vandalism, assault, and harassment should be prosecuted hard, whoever the victim is. That is not in question. The problem is codifying a contested political definition that reaches criticism of a foreign government, and applying it in education and criminal law. That is a speech standard wearing a civil rights label.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: One standard: conduct-based protection applied equally to every protected class, with no statutory definition that converts political argument into a violation. Synagogues and Jewish schools, mosques, Black churches, and Sikh gurdwaras have all been attacked in this country. Security funding should reach every congregation and religious school facing a credible threat, through one program, one application, one standard. I will expand that funding, not repeal it. Equal treatment means everyone is protected, not that nobody is. Florida runs foreign trade offices and state-backed innovation partnerships. They should exist under uniform published criteria, or not at all.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: No bilateral partnership that exists because of a political relationship rather than a Florida economic case. Every one reviewed against the same test, with results published, and closed where the case is not there. No foreign-government-backed facility or research partnership in Florida with plausible military application, from any country. Section 218.415 lists what local governments may buy with public money. The government of Israel is the only foreign government named in it. HB 669, effective July 1, 2025, went further. It bars a local government's own investment policy from requiring a minimum credit rating on those bonds. The statute's words are "Rated or unrated."

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: A county commission can no longer apply its own prudence standard to that one investment. Every investment of public money meets the same rating and risk standard, with no carve-out for any country. Local officials answer to local taxpayers. Tallahassee should not strip a county's ability to set its own prudence rules. Florida dollars should work in Florida first: infrastructure, workforce housing, local lending, American issuers. Public procurement is leverage. It should be governed by a written standard applied to every vendor, not by who has a relationship in Tallahassee.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: No state contract may fund a system whose ordinary operation violates the Fourth Amendment. Continuous tracking of people not under suspicion is the test, not the vendor's name. Toll collection and similar fixed-purpose cameras are permissible. They read a plate at a point of transaction. They do not build a movement history. Every surveillance contract published in full before signing, including retention periods, third-party access, and what the vendor may do with Florida data. No state contract with a company whose core business is building targeting or population-tracking systems for armed conflict. Applied by what the company builds, not by where it is based.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Human rights and conflict screening written as neutral criteria any vendor from any country can be measured against, published in advance, with an appeal. Florida and American vendors preferred where price and capability are comparable. The Florida Retirement System is what teachers, firefighters, police officers, and state workers retire on. They earned it by working for the public. Independent review of solvency, published in full: the unfunded liability, the assumed rate of return, and whether that assumption is honest. Review of fairness across tiers. People hired after a reform often carry worse terms for the same work, and nobody ever says that out loud at hiring.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Publish the investment portfolio, the external managers, the fees paid, and the performance net of those fees. An assumed return that nobody believes is a deferred tax increase on the next generation. Say the real number. No benefit promised that is not funded, and no fund raided to cover an unrelated budget hole. Every plan on this page is executed by people who work for the state, and a lot of those jobs are empty. Child welfare, corrections, nursing, inspections, and permitting are all running short. Vacancy rates, turnover, and time-to-fill published by agency and by position. You cannot fix what nobody is allowed to see.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Exit interviews conducted independently and the findings published in aggregate. Ask the people leaving why they left, and then believe them. Honest salary comparison against the private sector and against other states for the same work. Pay that fell behind and never caught up, so a veteran employee earns barely more than a new hire doing the same job. Caseloads set by the budget rather than by what one person can actually carry. Pension terms that got worse for anyone hired after a reform, for identical work. Fix those three and most of the recruiting problem solves itself. Keep ignoring them and no hiring bonus will hold. chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: License plate readers and mass surveillance # Automated license plate readers photograph every car that passes, not just the ones under suspicion. Your daily movements are recorded, stored, and searchable, and nobody asked you. End warrantless mass surveillance by ALPR networks in Florida. Order an audit of every ALPR and state surveillance system already deployed, including who has access and how long data is kept. The objection is Amber Alerts, stolen cars, fugitives, and trafficking. Those cases are handled with a warrant, strict use limits, short retention, and an audit trail. The current system tracks everyone to catch a few. That is the part that is backwards.

chunks.title: Issues · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Florida's constitutional right to privacy # Article I, Section 23 of the Florida Constitution gives Floridians a right to be let alone that stands independent of federal Fourth Amendment doctrine. Under the Winfield standard, the state must show a compelling interest and use the least intrusive means available. That protection exists on paper. It has not been enforced against modern surveillance systems. Florida's version is close to useless because of its billion-dollar revenue threshold. Almost no company has to comply. Require a one-click option that deletes everything a company holds on you.

chunks.title: About · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: No party bosses, no PAC money, no corporate donors. Just a plan, a record of getting things done, and a promise to say plainly what a governor can and can’t do. Candidate for Governor · No Party Affiliation · Sarasota I’ve spent about three decades in technology and consulting, working across the private and public sectors, including at Microsoft, HP and KPMG. After September 11, I helped rebuild New York City’s emergency communications. Since then I’ve led accountability and efficiency work for state governments, including here in Florida. I know how state agencies work from the inside, where the money goes, and how to make systems answer to the people who pay for them.

chunks.title: About · Dean Abrams for Governor
chunks.text: Outside of work, I’ve volunteered with charities serving people with disabilities, seniors, and people recovering from substance abuse. I’m running because the same problems keep getting worse — insurance, property taxes, housing, surveillance, our water — while both parties take money from the people who profit from them. I’m paying for this campaign myself and taking no party, PAC or corporate money, so the only people I owe are Floridians. Joe served eighteen years in the U.S. Air Force. Today he manages disaster-recovery projects, the work that matters most to Floridians after a storm. He is also an educator and coach who works with veterans and seniors.

chunks.text: Florida is growing. Businesses are coming here. People are moving here. But Frank believes there is a simple question we need to ask: Can the people who already live here afford to stay? chunks.title: Affordability Plan for Florida | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: Florida homeowners should not have to wonder whether the next insurance renewal will make their home unaffordable. chunks.title: Affordability Plan for Florida | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: Frank supports responsible property tax relief while protecting schools, public safety and essential services. His plan ties public support to real, measurable and lasting affordability. View Frank’s Housing Affordability Plan → Florida 9.9 - Invest in Florida’s Future

chunks.title: Affordability Plan for Florida | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: Frank believes in capitalism. He believes in entrepreneurship, building businesses, creating jobs and becoming extraordinarily successful.

chunks.title: Affordability Plan for Florida | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: He also believes extraordinary success comes with an opportunity to help keep Florida affordable for the people who teach our children, care for our families, build our homes and keep this state running. Ensuring local and state essential services for all Floridians also should not burden Floridian families (like property tax) in such a way that they are unable to build wealth for their children’s future. Frank's Florida 9.9 proposal would apply a 9.9% consumption state tax only to spending above $1 million. The first $1 million in spending would not be taxed, and implementation of this plan would require the approval from Florida voters through their elected representatives.

chunks.title: Affordability Plan for Florida | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: The revenue from this plan would be protected in public trust, not in government agency hands and reinvested in priorities including housing, teachers, healthcare workers, skilled trades and preparing Florida's workforce for AI and automation - with independent audits, public reporting and protections against politicians diverting the money elsewhere. Frank believes every affordability proposal should have to answer one question: Does this make it easier for Floridians to afford to build a life here? If the answer is no, we need to do better.

chunks.title: Immigration | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: Frank believes in secure borders. He believes in the rule of law. And as Governor, his first responsibility will always be keeping Floridians safe. But immigration is personal to Frank too. His family came to this country for the same reason generations of families have come here – for a chance to work hard, build a life and give their children something better. That’s why Frank doesn’t believe we have to choose between enforcing the law and treating people with dignity. Protect our communities. Follow the law. Support legal immigration. Treat people like human beings. We can do all four. Frank's first responsibility as Governor is to keep Floridians safe.

chunks.title: Immigration | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: That means focusing law enforcement resources on the people who actually threaten our communities - violent criminals, drug traffickers, human traffickers and transnational gangs. As Governor, Frank would strengthen partnerships between Florida law enforcement and federal agencies and prioritize state resources toward removing people who commit violent crimes and pose genuine threats to public safety. If you are a violent criminal, a trafficker or you're here to hurt people, we need to deal with that. There should be no question about it. Secure the Border - And Be Honest About Who Controls It Frank supports securing America's border.

chunks.title: Immigration | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: But he's also not going to pretend the Governor of Florida controls the United States border. Washington does. And Washington needs to do its job. Immigration is primarily a federal responsibility. A Florida governor cannot create citizenship, establish federal immigration status or single-handedly fix the nation's immigration system. What Florida can do is strengthen public safety partnerships, combat trafficking and exploitation, enforce the laws within its authority and make sure our state is doing its part. Frank believes leadership starts with being honest about what you can control - and then getting to work on it. Frank believes accountability has to go both ways.

chunks.title: Immigration | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: If a business or individual knowingly exploits undocumented workers or commits immigration-related fraud, they should be held accountable too. Frank would crack down on that exploitation while strengthening employment verification requirements for state agencies and state contractors so taxpayer-funded jobs comply with federal law. If you're breaking the law to exploit vulnerable workers, you don't get a free pass either. Frank believes legal immigration has helped build America. People who come here legally, work hard, follow the rules, raise families, build businesses and contribute to their communities should know that matters.

chunks.title: Immigration | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: Frank would expand English-language and workforce-development opportunities that help legal immigrants successfully integrate into Florida's economy. For Frank, this comes back to his own family's story. His family came to America looking for an opportunity to work hard and build something better for the next generation. That's part of Frank's story. And it's part of America's story. For too long, Washington has argued about immigration without fixing the system. Frank believes the federal government needs to secure the border, enforce the law and finally create a legal process that actually works.

chunks.title: Immigration | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: He supports calling on Congress to establish an earned federal process for long-term, law-abiding residents who meet strict legal requirements, including background checks and compliance with federal law. This isn't something Frank can create as Governor - and he won't pretend otherwise. But he can use Florida's voice to push Washington to act. Frank believes the principle should be clear: People who commit violent crimes should be removed. People who work hard, obey the law and contribute to their communities deserve a system that is fair, orderly and rooted in the rule of law. Frank doesn't believe Tallahassee has all the answers.

chunks.title: Immigration | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: He would establish a Governor's Immigration Advisory Council bringing together law enforcement, business leaders, agriculture, faith leaders, legal immigrants and local officials. chunks.title: Immigration | Russo-Rodriguez 2026

chunks.title: Children, Teachers & Trades | Russo-Rodriguez 2026

chunks.title: Children, Teachers & Trades | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: That's why he began the process of becoming a Florida substitute teacher - including completing the fingerprinting process - so he can experience today's classrooms firsthand and better understand what teachers and students are actually facing. chunks.title: Children, Teachers & Trades | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: His approach is to reduce administrative waste and redirect resources toward teachers and classrooms rather than allowing bureaucracy to continue growing. chunks.title: Children, Teachers & Trades | Russo-Rodriguez 2026

Not every successful career begins with a four-year college degree. Florida needs electricians, plumbers, HVAC technicians, construction professionals and skilled workers - and those careers can provide young Floridians with good-paying opportunities without requiring them to take on four years of college debt.

chunks.title: Children, Teachers & Trades | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: Frank wants to bring skilled-trades education back into Florida high schools so more students can graduate with certifications, practical skills and a direct path into the workforce. Artificial intelligence is going to change what work looks like. Frank believes Florida should prepare for that change rather than wait until workers are displaced by it. That means strengthening skilled careers that are difficult to automate while also preparing students and workers to participate in AI and emerging industries.

chunks.title: Children, Teachers & Trades | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: Frank's Florida 9.9 proposal would reinforce that investment through the protected Florida Future Fund - supporting teacher pay, skilled trades and apprenticeships, and education and retraining for workers affected by AI and automation. Frank's plan would expand technical training and create more paid apprenticeship opportunities connecting students directly with employers and skilled careers. He also wants experienced tradesmen and tradeswomen to have greater opportunities to teach the next generation - recognizing that decades of real-world experience can be just as valuable in a technical classroom as a traditional academic credential.

chunks.title: Children, Teachers & Trades | Russo-Rodriguez 2026
chunks.text: Students should be able to leave high school with more than a diploma. College. A trade. An apprenticeship. Entrepreneurship. A career. The goal is opportunity - not forcing every young Floridian down the same path. Frank doesn't believe the success of Florida's education system should be measured only by another ranking or report from Tallahassee. Are we attracting and keeping great teachers? Are our children prepared for life after graduation? Does every student have a path to a good-paying future? If we can answer yes, Florida is moving in the right direction.

chunks.text: Buying any policy is little more than an act of hope that it will actually pay the bills when you need it - and it probably won’t. What can be done? We absolutely, positively must return to basics. 1) Restore real incentives for doctors—driven out of private practice by crushing costs, litigation, insurance companies, and red tape—to reopen small offices, treat patients directly, and bill as they see fit. 2) Restore the sacred doctor-patient relationship, free from bureaucratic interference.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: 3) Rewrite the unaffordable, broken healthcare laws. Put doctors, not government and insurance companies, in charge. Make ‘Right to Try’ laws absolute. Affirm and codify “My Body, My Choice.” Free Florida medical research from bureaucratic and litigious strangulation. 4) Restore our insurance market back to pricing risk, reflected in policy premiums. 5) For healthy individuals with no pre-existing conditions - rebuild a genuine insurance market. Have Government create five clear, cookie-cutter standardized policy categories. For each category, create low-, medium-, and high-deductible versions—producing 15 easy-to-compare plans.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Insurers would then compete aggressively on price for each and offer them in the market: a. Diamond Plan – Covers every healthcare circumstance. b. Platinum Plan – Covers most healthcare circumstances. c. Gold Plan – Covers most healthcare circumstances, excluding accidents. d. Silver Plan – Covers only accidents, not routine health issues. e. Bronze Plan – Covers 50% of the cost of most healthcare incidents or accidents. For people with pre-existing conditions, there is no traditional insurance option. True insurance is protection against unknown future events, not pre-existing conditions.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: The truth is, the pre-existing conditions insurance term is nothing more than a government-mandated subsidy scheme, a forced wealth transfer from healthy people ( who pay grossly inflated premiums ) to people who are already sick. Slippery politicians want you to believe that it is just another form of insurance - it is not . Worse, forcing this scheme into a legitimate market/risk-based insurance system destroys the risk-based market that functioned for centuries hurting more people than it helps. That said, a responsible safety net is essential . It must however be deliberately engineered to minimize moral hazard, and it will require real creativity.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Leverage the insurance companies' expertise in managing costs and their strong negotiated rates with providers. Assign every person with a pre-existing condition to one of the insurers operating in the state. In return for a fair administrative fee, each company would manage, not pay for, care for an equal share of these patients. This 'care arrangement' would eliminate the crazy hospital pricing schemes, the extreme price shocks and anxiety patients face every day, like the well-known emergency room visit that gets billed to the patient for $21,000, and then is reduced for the insurance company to $1650! This one step alone could ignite a 'back to affordability' healthcare revolution!

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Every applicant would first be means-tested. Those who qualify could access a state-backed loan fund — up to $200,000 lifetime per person — administered jointly by the patient and their assigned insurer. Repayment would be capped at 28% of net income until the loan is repaid. For those who do not qualify, or whose needs exceed that lifetime limit , they would necessarily enter a tightly managed state pool overseen by physicians and medical experts who would directly coordinate their care and make cost-conscious treatment decisions.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: This plan keeps private insurers handling day-to-day administration and negotiation, uses loans instead of grants to reduce moral hazard, only applies full government control for the most extreme cases, and leaves the insurance market healthy, competing, and functioning with the most competitive premiums, exactly like it should function. Those newly competitive premiums, and easy to understand policies, could also induce the many who now go without coverage to go out and buy some! In other words, this plan would bring back “ real ” insurance coverage and aggressive competition, which will see premiums reflect actual risk – not the unknown costs of subsidizing a market with no visible bottom.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: It also provides for fair, compassionate and cost effective healthcare coverage for the most sick and needy among us. Affordable and workforce housing (AWH) are critical components of any successful community. Not everyone can afford market housing options, hence the need for AWH options. To begin, AWH should be located near to the communities they serve. However, some believe that AWH should be built inside the communities they serve. This is not ideal given the cost to build AWH in an already affluent community is extremely high and severely impacts the number and quality of the units that can be built.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: On the contrary, AWH built nearby, in blighted or lower income areas, has many benefits. Those benefits include the ability to buy land at lower costs, build more and better-quality units, transform the blighted and lower income areas with investments in the community, including roads, sidewalks, funds for better municipal services, new and better infrastructure, community activities and programs and many other benefits that go along with large investments in new projects. In short, AWH investment is desired and necessary. It should be used as a double-edged sword to both provide needed housing and improve needy areas. This way, taxpayers and recipients get the biggest bang for their buck!

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: This one is easy: take all steps necessary to make certain our water and air are clean and that Florida holds polluters accountable. Overcrowding in our State is taking hold in our large cities and traffic is approaching gridlock levels. The problem is that our leaders believe it is possible to put 10 pounds of population into a 5-pound population bag! It is not possible and is having the predictable effect. Florida needs to continue to invest in improving and enlarging where possible, its roadways. Florida also needs to look at common sense mass transportation alternatives like more rail, bus and other transportation modes which will help move our people from point to point.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: The real elephant in the room, however, is the massive population growth our State has experienced. As I said earlier, there is a limit to the number of people one can cram into a fixed area, and in much of our State, we have hit that limit. Stop building new housing until we can absorb the number of residents we currently have and start taking care of the Floridians who are already here and who deserve the quality of life they were promised and expect. In addition, rather than continue to build more new units, let’s fix the broken- and run-down units we already have, making housing better for all.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: If we stop making the problem worse by mindlessly adding more housing units, and fix and/or improve the housing units we already have, we might be able to preserve the amazing quality of life our current Florida residents envision, get our traffic nightmare under control and further increase the value of all our residents’ investment. All of that would be a home run for everyone. Our country is woefully overindebted and its retirement promises are unkeepable, as our Social Security and Medicare unfunded amounts alone are equal to 10 years' worth of every penny the United States collects in revenue! In other words, the system will fail, the only question is when?

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: We do not want this to happen to our retirees in Florida. While promises are nice, financial realities are something very different. The State of Florida has one pension system, the Florida Retirement System, (FRS). The mechanism for paying the aforementioned pension obligations is an investment account managed by the State. The required size of the investment account is determined by the revenue the account yields in relation to the number of retirees needing to be paid. Currently the account itself has become unable, on its own, to pay the amounts the State is required to pay.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Given same, in order to “fix” the pension system, the State would currently have to inject $43B into the fund, an amount equal to almost 50% of the State’s entire budget. Finally with respect to the above structure to pay retirees, in the case where the investment account begins to fail, is cut significantly or goes to zero, the State will likely bear the ENTIRE responsibility to come up with all of the funds, over $200B, a second time, to restore the investment account. Given the size of the investment account, this alone could bankrupt the State and devastate our taxpayers. The chances of this happening are not zero.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Contrast the above with a 401k type account for employees, with the State making very generous contributions; an account which each employee would own. Unlike the defined benefit plan first described above, the 401K type account is a defined contribution benefit plan. The 401k type plan has several benefits. 1) It allows the employee to own their account, benefit from it and take it with them with no strings attached. 2) Since the plan belongs to the employee they can invest and do with the funds in their account upon departure from the State as they wish.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: 3) It allows the State to pay as you go, budget responsibly, not go into debt and retain employees by raising the State’s contribution to a level which would entice and financially motivate its employees. Lastly a 401K type plan for all new employees, which is intelligently designed, would be good for those new employees, while honoring the promises made to existing employees, and at the same time protect Florida’s residents from making financial promises that they probably can’t afford to keep.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: The truth is, in the Free State of Florida, the high property tax rate is choking residents and enabling unconscious elected leaders in our cities and school boards to spend like the flow of money is never-ending. Given politicians are experts at talking, they will always have a reason why your paying more to them is necessary. Let's ignore that problem for a minute. Property owners deserve relief and unconscious elected leaders need to do the hard work of caring for taxpayer money, by cutting their overall budgets by at least 5% and preferably 10%. Floridians are continuously forced to tighten their belts, and the same should be required of government bureaucrats.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: For example, Florida school budgets have grown from $2.5 billion in 1980 to $29.7 billion in 2024, a 12-fold increase. Meanwhile the 1980 median income for the average Floridian was about $18,000, and in 2024 that number grew to $72,000, only a 4-fold increase. Worse the number of people living in Florida expected to pay for the 12-fold increase in school budgets has only about doubled since 1980. The real question is, how do Floridians pay any bill that has gone up 12-times, with personal income that has only increased 4-times? What’s the solution and how to implement it? Slash and eventually eliminate property taxes for residency vested Florida homeowners and renters.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: For each year beyond a year-ten residency vesting period requirement, Florida homeowners would be entitled to a cumulative 10%-point increase of their existing homestead exemption, until their adjusted exemption reaches 100%. Renters in Florida, who meet the ten-year residency vesting period requirement and who go on to purchase a Florida home, would also enjoy the same cumulative 10%-point increase of their new home's homestead exemption, until their adjusted exemption reaches 100%. Additionally and critically, the adjusted homestead exemption shall be transferable to the homeowner's wife or children. 1) Immediately reduce the Florida Constitutional maximum property tax rate by 50%.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: This change would mean the potential maximum tax rate on one’s property would be necessarily dramatically reduced thereby reducing revenue to government by up to $18B. 2) Reduce school spending by at least 5%, possibly 10%, directing those savings to property owners, reducing revenue to government by $1.5B to $3B. 3) Reduce municipal spending by at least 5%, possibly 10%, saving property owners and reducing revenue to government by $1.5B to $3B. 4) Reduce fraud and waste Statewide likely saving $3B to $5B. 5) Other miscellaneous State and municipal savings of $1B.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: 6) Note: Florida had a $21B surplus in its most recent budget. These funds should be added to Florida’s version of a savings account for emergencies only, the Budget Stabilization Fund (BSF). 7) Last but not least, the law must be changed to allow homesteaded property owners the right to pass down properties to wives and children, without an increase in assessed value - which would otherwise make a family home instantly unaffordable and ensure that Florida families will all be involuntarily displaced.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: By taking all of the above-mentioned steps, the likely result would be that property values would increase, revenues to government would necessarily increase, property owners would receive desperately needed relief and government would be forced to spend the revenue it collects much more carefully. Legal immigration is good. Uncontrolled, unvetted, unregulated, illegal immigration is bad. I support the responsible development of AI in Florida, provided it delivers clear benefits to Floridians and does not come at the expense of any of our residents. To that end, I would require the following conditions for any new data center:

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: As a condition of approval, each data center must commit to building or funding additional power generation and infrastructure sufficient to supply at least 120% of its actual power consumption. This obligation would remain in effect for the entire life of the project. Additionally, data centers would be required to pay 110% of the electricity rate charged to residential customers, or 110% of the rate they normally pay, whichever is greater. The extra 10% would be credited back on a pro-rata basis to Florida’s residential ratepayers. Supercharging Florida’s Forgotten – Tough Love Will Work Here, Just Like it Does at Home.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Florida’s poor don’t need another handout. They need a real shot — and the support to seize it. We have too many voiceless brothers and sisters trapped in slums, ghettos, and war-zone neighborhoods that no one should have to endure. Enough is enough. We’re done subsidizing failure. We’re done watching good tax dollars vanish into programs that reward dependency and punish success. The failed “Live Local Act” and its clones are a disgrace: they deliver almost zero low-cost housing for struggling Floridians, bulldoze historic neighborhoods, and stuff millions into the pockets of connected developers and politicians. It’s corporate welfare dressed up as compassion.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Enter my proposed “Oasis Act” — a no-excuses, results-driven revolution. Instead of scattering money to the wind, the Oasis Act redirects the exact same developer incentives to the worst, most dangerous, and forgotten slum parcels across Florida where the land is dirt-cheap. That means every state dollar stretches dramatically farther — and actually changes lives. Ironclad security first. A hardened perimeter seals the entire site. One way in, one way out, with 24/7 security at the gate. Outside predators, gangs, drugs, and chaos are kept out. Period.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Safe, dignified housing rises next — clean, affordable units for families who want better. Parks, playgrounds, and real neighborhood features included. Limited retail and offices go in — just enough to supply daily needs inside the Oasis. Residents will still do most of their shopping and work in the wider world. Rigorous rules. Every resident signs on to accountability: no crime, no drugs, school attendance for kids, work or training requirements for adults. Break the rules, and your spot is given to another willing to follow the rules. This isn’t a free ride — it’s a launchpad for serious and committed people who are ready to climb.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Once the first Oasis proves it works, we replicate it aggressively until every blighted war zone area in Florida is transformed. One day the walls come down, the gates open, and what was a dangerous slum becomes another safe, thriving Florida neighborhood. Bottom line: This is the biggest bang for the taxpayer housing buck Florida has ever seen. It gives our most disadvantaged citizens, who are willing to be accountable, a genuine, life-changing gateway out of poverty — not another trap disguised as “help.” It gives our disadvantaged Floridians the tools, the safety, and the tough love they actually need to win.

chunks.title: Burkett for FL Governor
chunks.text: Florida deserves better. Our poorest deserve a real chance — and the rest of us deserve policies that finally work and rid our state of the blight that ruins the lives of too many. For even more information on where I stand on the issues, click the white button. Want to know my views on various subjects? Help fuel our success by getting our word out! chunks.text: Experience, Common Sense & Compassion Charles Burkett Experience, Common Sense & Compassion Charles Burkett Born in Costa Rica to Cuban parents who fled the Castro regime, Ruben arrived in the United States as an infant. He has lived in Florida his entire life, spending more than three decades in the beautiful town of Surfside. It is in this state that Ruben and his wife, Lea Baruch, chose to raise their two sons, Joseph and Gabriel. Leveraging his background in real estate, finance, and insurance, Ruben is focused on actionable statewide economic goals designed to lower the cost of living for all Floridians. His key priorities include:

chunks.title: My pick for Lt. Governor
chunks.text: Stabilizing the Property Insurance Market: Driving down soaring premiums through transparent, market-stabilizing reforms that protect homeowners instead of special interests. Making Florida Affordable (Again): There are too many people in and coming to Florida who are competing for limited resources. We need to stop importing new Florida residents and first take care of the ones who live here now. Slash government fees, costs and fines, phase out property taxes for homesteaders and current renters who will buy. Tolls and HOV lanes will be eliminated, saving drivers time and money.

chunks.title: My pick for Lt. Governor
chunks.text: Cutting Red Tape for Small Businesses: Eliminating burdensome regulations and hidden costs that prevent local entrepreneurs from thriving. Protecting Taxpayer Dollars: Ensuring strict fiscal accountability and responsible spending so tax dollars are reinvested directly into infrastructure, flooding defense, and community safety.

chunks.title: My pick for Lt. Governor

For the past 13 years, he has continued his business leadership in the insurance sector as the owner of Coto Industries LLC, specializing in health and life insurance. This deep professional background gives Ruben firsthand knowledge of the economic needs, financial responsibilities, and hard work required by Florida's families and small business owners.

chunks.title: My pick for Lt. Governor
chunks.text: Ruben’s passion for civic engagement is rooted in a proven track record of local leadership, highlighted by his service across two terms as a Surfside Town Commissioner . During his tenure on the commission, he fought to protect his community from overdevelopment, championed equal code enforcement, and worked directly to resolve critical infrastructure and flooding issues.

chunks.title: My pick for Lt. Governor

His extensive local involvement also includes serving on Parks and Recreation committees, the Surfside Business Association, and working with public information programs focused on flood education and safety. Additionally, guided by 13 years of service as a Cub Scout and Boy Scout leader, Ruben operates with a strict code of being helpful, trustworthy, and courteous. chunks.title: Jose Javier Rodriguez
chunks.text: Rodríguez Draws Sharp Contrast as Insurance Industry Backs Republican Attorney General Miami, FL.- The Associated Industries of Florida (AIF), a powerful business lobbying group that represents Florida’s insurance and corporate interests, announced this week its endorsement of Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier.

chunks.title: Jose Javier Rodriguez
chunks.text: With legislative leaders already signaling that no meaningful property insurance reforms are expected this year, Floridians are being told to wait - again - while costs continue to rise. At moments like this, consumers should be able to rely on an Attorney General to enforce the law and hold insurance companies accountable. Instead, Florida has an Attorney General who sides with corporate and insurance interests rather than using the full authority of the office to protect families and homeowners. José Javier Rodríguez, Democratic candidate for Florida Attorney General, said the endorsement underscores a clear choice facing voters this November.

chunks.title: Jose Javier Rodriguez
chunks.text: “There is a clear difference between my opponent and me,” said Rodríguez . “While my opponent is being endorsed by insurance and corporate interests, I am committed to representing Florida families and workers. When the Legislature won’t act and powerful interests are calling the shots, the Attorney General has a responsibility to step up, not protect powerful industries, but hold them accountable and stand up for people who don’t have an army of lobbyists working on their behalf.”

chunks.title: Jose Javier Rodriguez
chunks.text: Rodríguez has made consumer protection, accountability, and affordability central to his campaign, emphasizing that too often powerful interests, including insurance companies and utilities, have gone unchecked while costs for everyday Floridians continue to rise.

chunks.title: Jose Javier Rodriguez
chunks.text: In recent weeks, Rodríguez has earned the support of a growing list of respected leaders known for enforcing the law and protecting consumers, including former Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth, former U.S. Senator Bill Nelson, former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg, former Miami Beach Mayor Dan Gelber, former Florida Chief Financial Officer Alex Sink, and former state legislator and former Florida Attorney General candidate Sean Shaw. chunks.text: Rodríguez Slams Uthmeier for Taking Big Tobacco and Gun Industry Money While Floridians Face Rising Costs Miami, FL - Following new reporting detailing major contributions from Big Tobacco and a gun manufacturer to Attorney General James Uthmeier’s campaign, Democratic candidate for Attorney General José Javier Rodríguez criticized Uthmeier for prioritizing powerful special interests over Florida families. That tells you everything you need to know about who he’s working for, and why Floridians aren’t seeing relief,” said José Javier Rodríguez. “Floridians deserve an Attorney General who stands up to corporate abuse, not one funded by it. As Attorney General, I’ll be the people’s lawyer - focused on lowering costs, protecting consumers, and holding powerful interests accountable.”

chunks.title: Jose Javier Rodriguez

chunks.title: Jose Javier Rodriguez
chunks.text: Statement from José Javier Rodríguez, Candidate for Florida Attorney General, on “Alligator Alcatraz” James Uthmeier’s so-called “Alligator Alcatraz” isn’t a serious plan, it’s a reckless, rushed project that puts lives and resources at risk. Detaining immigrants at a remote airfield in the Everglades, with no clear legal framework or due process, is about fear, not safety. The most obvious reason seems to be political theater, just trying to get attention in Washington, rather than looking out for the interests of our state and its people.

chunks.title: Jose Javier Rodriguez
chunks.text: Now they’re funding it with FEMA dollars - money meant to help us prepare for hurricanes and natural disasters, especially in a state like Florida. And let’s be clear: this isn’t just irresponsible - it’s a rushed plan cloaked in secrecy by using emergency powers. It will not be surprising to see if some well-connected friends of Uthmeier profit from this. We need leadership that respects the law, protects people’s rights, and focuses on real public safety, not political deals and fear tactics. chunks.title: Jose Javier Rodriguez
chunks.text: Statement from José Javier Rodríguez on Uthmeier’s Refusal to Comply with Court Order on Everglades Detention Center Today, José Javier Rodríguez, Democratic candidate for Florida Attorney General, released the following statement after recent news on the Everglades detention center and Attorney General James Uthmeier’s refusal to comply with a court order to shut down the facility: “Florida’s Attorney General should defend the law, not defy it.
