chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly Florida Should Be a Place You Can Afford to Call Home From the rent check to the insurance bill, the cost of living here has outrun the paychecks of the people who make Florida run.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Our plan takes on Florida's affordability crisis in several ways. Let's start with housing and insurance.It dramatically lowers insurance premiums by creating a statewide catastrophic fund. It reduces monthly electric bills by capping utility company profits. It scales up workforce and affordable housing construction with down-payment assistance for first-time buyers. Our plan protects renters through expanded affordable housing programs and, to help condo owners cover special assessments, it offers no-interest state-backed loans. It's an actual plan, not an empty promise, to leave Florida families with more money at the end of each month.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: For generations, Florida meant a fresh start, a house with a yard, and the room to build a life. Now young families are watching that promise fade as the typical first-time buyer waits until age 40, and even lifelong Floridians open their insurance bills with dread. This is not just an economic problem. It is about whether working people can still put down roots in the state they love.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: No family should have to choose between insuring their home and keeping the lights on. Florida pays the highest homeowners' premiums in the country, and too many carriers have walked away, leaving people stranded. We will fight for a system that treats hurricane risk as the shared statewide challenge it is, so a single storm season doesn't decide whether you keep your house. Read the full plan: how a state-backed catastrophe fund cuts Florida homeowners insurance by 60 to 70 percent.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Electricity is not a luxury, and over-the-top profits for the biggest utilities should not come out of your monthly budget. Florida regulators have let investor-owned power companies earn some of the fattest returns in the nation while families ration the air conditioning in the summer heat. We will push to cap utility profits in line with the national average and put that money back where it belongs, in your pocket.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: You cannot fix a shortage by wishing it away, and Florida is short the homes its growing families need. We will invest in the tools that work, from workforce housing to real down-payment help for first-time buyers, so a nurse, a teacher, or a young couple can find a place they can afford. Building more is how we bring prices back within reach. Protect Renters and Condo Owners Left Behind

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Half of Florida renters now hand over more than a third of their income just to keep a roof overhead, and older condo owners are being hit with special assessments that can wipe out a lifetime of savings. Safety matters, and no one should live in an unsafe building, but families cannot be left to shoulder impossible bills alone. We will stand with renters and long-time owners so the fine print doesn't force them out of their own homes.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: When most people can't cover a surprise bill without going into debt, the whole economy is one storm away from crisis. Real affordability means an honest shot at saving, not just surviving the next deductible or rate hike. Every fight on this page comes back to one goal: leaving Florida families with more at the end of the month. Florida can be a place where hard work still buys a home, a full fridge, and a night's sleep without worry. Let's build that Florida together. Q. Why can't I afford to buy a home in Florida anymore?

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Florida's median home price reached $420,000, mortgage rates sit around 6.36 percent, and insurance premiums are among the nation's highest. Long-term owners pay far less property tax than new buyers for the same house thanks to Save Our Homes caps, and the structural result is that the median first-time buyer age has risen sharply. Q. How will this plan help me if I rent? More than half of Florida renters now pay over 30 percent of income on housing. The plan scales workforce and affordable housing targeted near job centers, expands existing state housing programs, and caps utility profits to lower the monthly bills renters pay on top of rent.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. What if I own an older condo and got hit with a huge special assessment? Older coastal condos have been hit hardest by new inspection requirements, with many owners facing assessments of $50,000 or more per unit. The plan offers no-interest state-backed loans so associations can spread costs over time without forcing fixed-income owners to sell. Q. What if I am a hospitality worker in Tampa or Orlando? The plan specifically calls for scaling workforce housing based on income and proximity to work, deliberately targeting tourism corridors rather than scattered housing. The utility profit cap would also lower monthly bills, and the proximity to work framing should reduce commute costs.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. What are average home insurance premiums in Florida right now? Estimates range from roughly $5,400 to $15,000 per year depending on home value and coverage level. Every credible analysis ranks Florida at or near the top nationally, with coastal markets like Miami-Dade, Tampa, and Jacksonville seeing the largest increases. Q. Won't capping utility profit hurt investment in Florida's grid? The cap would bring Florida's authorized utility return in line with the national average of roughly 9 to 10 percent. Utilities in other states earning that rate continue to invest in grid modernization and storm hardening, there is no evidence that matching the national norm suppresses investment.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. Will a state catastrophic insurance fund just be a taxpayer bailout for risky homes? No, it is a risk-pooling mechanism that lowers costs for everyone by spreading hurricane exposure across all Florida homes. Homeowners still pay for their state hurricane coverage, just at a lower combined cost than today's system where each private insurer prices in huge risk margins. Q. What about retirees on fixed income in Florida?

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Retirees face acute pressures from condo special assessments and rising property insurance. The no-interest state-backed condo loan is targeted directly at fixed-income condo owners who can't absorb a six-figure special assessment, and the catastrophic fund insurance savings would also hit hardest for retirees who often pay insurance directly. In depth The Florida I Remember (And What We're Losing) In depth As Governor - Affordability Housing

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly No one should be one diagnosis away from fear, delay, or debt. David Jolly's health care plan for Florida expands Medicaid to cover hundreds of thousands of uninsured Floridians and invests in more primary care clinics throughout the state so people can access care when and where they need it, regardless of income. Medicaid expansion can start within months once the Legislature approves it, with coverage beginning in the first year. Jolly proposes a five-year pilot to dramatically expand community health centers in every Florida county so care is available, not just coverage on paper. A Plan as Governor to Improve Health Care

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: This system isn't working for the people who need it. Across Florida, families are making impossible choices when it comes to health care. Going without insurance. Delaying treatment. Hoping that what they are dealing with doesn't get worse. Not because they don't care about their health. But because the system makes it too expensive, too complicated, and too uncertain. No one should have to wonder whether they can afford to get care. No one should be forced to choose between their health and their financial stability. And yet, that's exactly where too many people find themselves.

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Expanding Medicaid is part of the solution. It would provide coverage to hundreds of thousands of Floridians who are currently left without access to care. Because access isn't just about coverage. It's about whether care is actually available when and where people need it. That's why Florida should invest in more primary healthcare clinics throughout the state. Places where people can go, regardless of income, to receive basic care, support, and treatment. Not as a long-term substitute for a better system. But as a way to make sure people aren't left waiting while bigger solutions take shape. Health care should be built around people. Not barriers.

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: And right now, there are too many barriers standing in the way. Getting care shouldn't feel like a risk. It should feel within reach for every Floridian. Join the fight for accessible health care in Florida Real solutions start with real action. Stand with David Jolly to expand health care access across Florida. Q. Why isn't Medicaid expansion enough on its own? Because expansion provides coverage, but people still need somewhere to actually get care. Jolly proposes a 5-year pilot to dramatically expand community health centers in every Florida county so new enrollees can connect with primary care providers, not just have coverage on paper.

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. How long would this plan take to actually help me? Medicaid expansion can start within months once the Legislature approves it, with coverage beginning in the first year. Scaling community health centers takes longer, which is why Jolly proposes a 5-year build to create durable access alongside the immediate coverage. Q. Does this plan raise my taxes as a Florida resident? No. The plan uses Florida tax dollars already being collected, paired with a 9-to-1 federal match. The state share is offset by reduced emergency care costs, lower uncompensated care payments, and increased tax revenue from a stronger healthcare workforce. Q. How would this plan affect rural Floridians?

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Rural counties have been hit hardest by healthcare gaps. Jolly's plan scales community health centers in every county, including rural areas where private practices are unviable, and stabilizes rural hospital revenue by reducing uncompensated care through Medicaid expansion. Q. What if I am a small business owner in Florida? Small businesses struggle to offer coverage because they cannot get the group rates large employers negotiate. Medicaid expansion would let your lowest-paid workers have a coverage option instead of being stuck in the coverage gap, and it stabilizes the market where you and your employees buy insurance. Q. How does Florida rank for healthcare nationally?

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Poorly across most measures. Florida has one of the highest uninsured rates in the country at 15.5% for working-age adults, ranks among the worst states for maternal mortality, and has about 266,000 adults shut out of both Medicaid and marketplace subsidies. Q. What if the federal government cuts the 90% match?

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: The 90% match is set in statute, not annual appropriation, which means it cannot be changed without an act of Congress. Any change would also disrupt 41 states' Medicaid programs, including red states like Indiana and Ohio, which makes a partisan cut politically difficult. Florida could adopt trigger provisions that would automatically roll back expansion if the federal match drops below a certain level. Q. How would this plan affect Florida hospitals?

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Florida hospitals would see two direct benefits. First, Medicaid expansion would shift much of the uncompensated care burden to the federal government at the 90% match rate. Second, scaling community health centers reduces preventable ER visits by triaging patients in primary care. In depth Why Florida's Next Governor Will Fire the Surgeon General

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida Public education shouldn't be an afterthought. Florida families deserve real opportunity. And that starts with strong public schools. David Jolly believes public education should be Florida's foundation, not an afterthought. His plan focuses on paying teachers what they deserve, investing in school infrastructure and resources, and ensuring every child has access to strong public schools regardless of zip code. He argues Florida needs a public education renaissance, not abandonment, because strong public schools strengthen communities, support families, and build the workforce Florida's future depends on.

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: This isn't what real school choice looks like. For years, Florida politicians have talked about school choice as if it is the answer to everything. But for many families, that “choice” doesn’t actually exist. Because when public schools are underfunded, understaffed, and left behind, families aren’t choosing between great options. And too often, that system has shifted education into the hands of for-profit institutions, while the public schools that serve the majority of Florida’s children are asked to do more with less. That’s not a real solution. It’s a system that leaves too many students behind.

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Public education should be the foundation. The place where every child, regardless of zip code, has access to opportunity, support, and a real path forward. But that only happens when we invest in it. That means paying teachers what they deserve. Supporting the people who show up every day to educate, guide, and inspire the next generation. It means investing in school infrastructure, classrooms, and resources so students aren’t trying to learn in systems that have been neglected for too long. And it means recognizing that strong public schools don’t just benefit students. They strengthen communities, support families, and build the workforce that Florida’s future depends on.

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Florida doesn’t need to abandon public education. That starts with schools we are willing to invest in. Get involved in the fight for Florida's public schools Q. Why are so many teachers leaving Florida? Florida opened the 2024-25 school year with nearly 10,000 vacant positions, including over 5,000 teacher roles. The main reason is pay: Florida's average teacher salary ranks 50th of 51 states nationally (only Mississippi is worse), and teachers also cite high cost of living and Florida's political climate as reasons to leave. Q. What does Jolly want to do about teacher pay?

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Jolly wants to dramatically increase teacher pay as part of a 10-year public education renaissance. He proposes redirecting Tourist Development Tax revenue (currently used for convention centers and tourism promotion) toward teacher pay and school infrastructure, which would require legislative change. Q. How does Jolly plan to fund his education priorities? Jolly proposes expanding the allowed uses of Florida's Tourist Development Tax (over $1 billion per year statewide) to include teacher pay and school infrastructure. His framing: Florida doesn't have a crisis of convention centers, it has a crisis of public education. Q. What about rural Florida school districts?

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Rural districts face compounding challenges: shrinking enrollment, higher per-pupil costs, and the most severe teacher shortages (especially in special education, science, and math). Jolly's plan to raise teacher pay statewide would help rural districts compete for talent, and expanded state funding would help them maintain operations as local tax bases decline. Q. How are Florida public schools currently funded? Florida K-12 public schools are funded primarily through the Florida Education Finance Program (FEFP), which combines state appropriations, local property tax revenue, and federal funds. Florida's per-pupil spending is approximately $12,400, ranking 8th lowest among U.S. states.

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Q. Is the federal government taking over education policy? No. Federal funding is under 10% of total K-12 spending, and federal law explicitly gives states control over curriculum, funding, teacher policy, and school choice. State-level governance (governor and legislature) is the dominant driver of school quality, which is why a Florida governor's education plan has more impact on Florida students than any federal change.

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly David Jolly believes protecting Florida's environment is essential to the state's economy and quality of life. His plan calls for real investments in environmental protection, accelerated clean and renewable energy integration into Florida's utility system, sustained funding for coastal resiliency and water quality improvements, and honest climate planning in state policy. David sees environmental protection as protecting what makes Florida successful: the tourism economy, clean beaches, healthy waters, and the natural beauty that families depend on every day. This is about more than the environment.

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: For families across Florida, the environment isn't an abstract issue. It's part of everyday life. It's the beaches they visit and parks they play in. The water they drink and air they breathe. The places that make this state feel like home. For David and his family, it's deeply personal. Time spent near the ocean, watching their kids experience the same natural beauty that defines so much of Florida. That connection is something millions of Floridians share. And yet, too often, protecting it is treated like a secondary concern. Something to debate. Something to delay. But the truth is, Florida's environment isn't separate from its success.

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Our economy depends on it. Tourism. Fishing. Local businesses. Entire communities rely on clean water, healthy coastlines, and a natural environment that people want to experience and protect. When that is threatened, it's not just an environmental issue. It's an economic one. It's a quality of life issue. It's a future issue. Protecting Florida's environment means making real investments. Taking real responsibility. And refusing to treat long-term damage as acceptable. It means understanding that what we protect today is what we pass on tomorrow. Because once it's gone, it's not coming back. Florida's future depends on what we protect today. Q. Is my insurance crisis related to climate?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Yes, structurally. Florida's property insurance crisis is driven by hurricane risk, litigation costs, and reinsurance prices, and the hurricane risk component has grown with warming ocean temperatures and rising sea levels. Insurers price policies to absorb rising expected losses, so climate is one of the underlying drivers of the insurance crisis. Yes, and Florida faces some of the most direct climate impacts in the country. Florida's Gulf Coast is projected for 22 to 26 inches of sea level rise by 2050 (about double the U.S. average), and hurricane intensity is rising. The 2024 hurricane season caused over $100 billion in combined damage across the Southeast.

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. What does David Jolly want to do about clean energy? Jolly's position is to unleash clean and renewable energies across Florida, requiring greater integration of clean energy technologies into public utilities. This means stronger net metering rules to support rooftop solar and accelerated utility-scale renewable buildout. Florida is projected to receive $62.7 billion in IRA-funded clean power investment by 2030. Q. Aren't climate policies just going to hurt the Florida economy?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: The economic case runs the other way. Florida's tourism economy ($134 billion in visitor spending, 1.8 million jobs), ocean economy, and saltwater fishing industry ($9.2 billion in annual impact) all depend on a healthy environment. Climate policy in Florida protects the state's largest industries rather than imposing costs against them. Q. What about Floridians who live in coastal communities?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Coastal Floridians face the most direct climate exposure: rising sea levels, more intense hurricanes, and accelerating beach erosion. David Jolly's plan calls for wiser coastal development practices and sustained investment in resiliency, which means living shorelines and hybrid systems, seawalls where necessary and appropriate, raised infrastructure, beach renourishment where cost-effective and sustainable, stormwater drainage upgrades, and building code modernization in coastal counties. Q. How would David Jolly handle Florida's water quality crises?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Jolly's plan ties water quality to broader environmental investment. Blue-green algae crises are addressed by reducing discharges of nutrient pollution to our coastal waters, and springs degradation is addressed through septic to sewer conversions, agricultural runoff rules, and groundwater protection. Protecting Florida's coast requires changing what flows into it. Q. What about FPL and renewable energy under David Jolly?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Jolly's clean energy position would require greater integration of renewables into Florida's utility planning. That likely means stronger net metering rules to support rooftop solar and accelerated utility-scale renewable buildout, pushing FPL and other utilities to expand renewable generation. Q. Why oppose offshore drilling if it could create Florida jobs?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Offshore drilling creates very few Florida jobs because rigs are based out of Louisiana and Texas ports. What Florida loses in a spill (tourism revenue, fishing industry, real estate value, ecological damage) runs to tens of billions of dollars. Florida's tourism economy ($130 billion) and ocean economy ($30 billion) depend on clean beaches and healthy water.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026 Before the labels. Before the noise. There's the person and the choices that shaped him. David Jolly is a former Member of Congress, attorney, and fifth-generation Floridian running for Florida Governor in 2026. His campaign focuses on historic homeowner's insurance reform, expanding primary healthcare services, and investing in community public schools. Jolly believes everyone deserves access to work, wages, and wealth, with rights protected and dignity celebrated regardless of background. People will try to tell you who David Jolly is. This page lets you hear it for yourself. Not through labels. Not through talking points.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: Chapter One: Not a politician. A person. Before anything else, this starts with the person. Faith, family, and where you come from shape what you carry forward. That matters as much as what you believe now. Chapter Three: This moment needs something different. You do not step forward because you want the title. You step forward because the moment demands change. Growing means being willing to choose what is right over what is expected. Change is not weakness. It is strength.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: David Jolly is a former Member of Congress, attorney, and nationally recognized television analyst who launched his bid for Governor in June of 2025. Since announcing his candidacy, David has traveled every corner of the state, hosting hundreds of town halls and community forums focused on improving the state’s economy. A person of deep faith, David believes everyone deserves a shot at work, wages, and wealth, and that their rights should be protected and their dignity celebrated, regardless of the color of one’s skin, where they were born, who they love, or who they worship.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: David has focused his campaign on historic groundbreaking homeowner’s insurance reform, the expansion of primary healthcare services, and investing in more community public schools. A fifth-generation Floridian and son of a minister, David and his wife Laura are raising their young family in Pinellas County.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: David’s political story is one of change. While in Congress, he was known as a common-sense Republican working across the aisle on issues like campaign finance reform, gun violence prevention, reproductive freedom, and the environment. His fight to take on Washington corruption was featured on CBS’ 60 Minutes. David then spent seven years as an independent, organizing voters throughout the country around democracy protection, ending gerrymandering, opening primaries, and reforming our broken campaign finance laws.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: Today, David is a proud Florida Democrat, fighting for the values he sees rooted in democratic tradition, that the economy should work for everyone; responsible investments in housing, healthcare, and education can improve people’s lives; and, everyone’s rights should be protected regardless of their walk of life. David’s willingness to lead with conviction led the Tampa Bay Times to write, “It’s refreshing to hear someone take on the system.” One Washington Post columnist famously penned, “Jolly speaks the truth.” And upon leaving Congress, another columnist wrote, “Farewell to the one Congressman willing to compromise.”

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: In addition to his work in Congress and in the private practice of law, David served for nearly a decade as a political analyst on NBC and MSNBC. His work has been featured in Time, USA Today, Roll Call, The Washington Post, The New York Times, CNN, NBC, and The Tampa Bay Times. David received a Bachelor’s degree from Emory University and a Juris Doctor Cum Laude from George Mason. chunks.title: About - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Trump-endorsed candidate for Florida Governor. Brooklyn-born, Naples-raised family man, and a conservative who has never had to be talked into the fight. A single-parent household in Brooklyn. Every sacrifice his mother could make. One American Dream. Born and raised in Brooklyn, New York, Byron Donalds is the product of a single-parent household. Throughout his life, his mother made every sacrifice possible to give him the best opportunity to live the American Dream. That philosophy his mother taught him, striving to leave future generations better than the current, is what leads him in his work, his home life, and as a Member of Congress.

chunks.title: About - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Byron attended Florida State University and graduated in 2002 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in finance and marketing. His career path included work in the finance, insurance, and banking industries in Southwest Florida. While serving in the Florida House of Representatives, Byron made his mark as a champion for school choice and parental rights in education, leading the effort to enact Hope Scholarships and passing a first-in-the-nation bill allowing parents and community members to review instructional materials in schools. He chaired the House Insurance and Banking Subcommittee and was appointed by Governor Rick Scott to the Board of Trustees for Florida SouthWestern State College.

chunks.title: About - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Since 2020, Donalds has served the people of Florida's 19th Congressional District, quickly distinguishing himself as a conservative warrior, standing against the rise of woke culture in schools, corporate America, the financial services industry, and the military. He is a staunch advocate for the Second Amendment, school choice, fiscal sanity, secure borders, law and order, and limited federal government, consistently earning the highest ratings from conservative organizations. Donalds served as a top surrogate for the 2024 Trump campaign and fought to hold the Biden administration accountable.

chunks.title: Education - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: “Reading by third grade is a basic promise every child deserves. Every student should Read to Succeed, stay active and healthy, and have a debt-free route to a great-paying job.” Train future teachers in proven phonics and reading science so every classroom teaches reading the right way. Catch reading issues early in Kindergarten through 2nd grade, before children fall behind. Provide free, state-funded tutoring for every 3rd grader struggling with reading. Reward top-performing reading teachers with real bonus pay for getting results. Bring back real books in the classroom instead of parking young kids in front of screens all day.

chunks.title: Education - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Connect high schools and community colleges with local businesses to offer paid apprenticeships in construction, advanced manufacturing, and defense. Help young Floridians step straight into careers earning around $60,000 a year without taking on piles of student debt. Students and businesses lead not government bureaucracy Personalized Success Plans for Every Student: Every student gets a tailored success plan no later than 6th grade, with annual updates through graduation. College, university, workforce/trade, military, entrepreneurship, and hybrid pathways are equally resourced and equally respected.

chunks.title: Education - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Families are co-authors, not bystanders. Annual plan reviews include parent conversations. Internship, apprenticeship, and industry certification milestones are baked into each plan, not treated as add-ons. Transparency for parents means schools are held accountable so that each student is receiving a plan to express their God-given talents. No more education factories or status quo. Strong Kids, Strong Florida (Physical Fitness): Bring back the Presidential Fitness Test to build healthy habits and keep kids active throughout the school day. Give mini-grants to schools that encourage regular daily recess and structured physical activity.

chunks.title: Education - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Send fitness scores straight home to mom and dad, keeping children's private health data out of state databases. Let education money follow the student so parents can choose the best school for their child. Keep partisan political theories out of the classroom so schools focus strictly on the basics: reading, math, and science.

chunks.title: Affordability - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Affordability - Byron Donalds for Governor “Florida cannot become too expensive for working families and seniors on fixed incomes. The status quo has a cost. Progress doesn't pay the bill sitting on your kitchen counter today—it's time to bring down costs.” Protect reforms and stop lawsuit abuse that jacks up rates for everyone, saving homeowners hundreds of dollars a year. Lower costs by trimming down state fees when reserves are full so those extra dollars stay in your wallet. Pursue regulatory reforms that lower insurance premiums. Reform the My Safe Florida Home program and other grants programs to fund real, storm-hardening upgrades that lower your annual premium the most.

chunks.title: Affordability - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Keep Citizens Insurance small so everyday drivers and homeowners never get hit with a surprise "hurricane tax" bill after a big storm. Cut the red tape and slow permitting that make rebuilding a home after a storm needlessly expensive and drive up your insurance premiums. Hold Insurance Companies Accountable—Put Consumers First: Create a simple online Scorecard where you can compare insurance companies side by side on price, how fast they pay claims, and how often they deny coverage. Require insurers to report accurate data or pay real fines, keeping the tool free for taxpayers by having the insurance industry cover the cost.

chunks.title: Affordability - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Keep property taxes in check so seniors and working families aren't taxed out of their homes. Stop giant industrial data centers from passing their massive electric and water bills onto everyday households.

chunks.title: Healthcare - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: “You deserve to know what healthcare costs before you get treated. Your Doctor, Your Price puts you back in charge, cuts out the red tape, and lets doctors focus on their patients.” Require doctors and hospitals to post plain, guaranteed cash prices for the 50 most common medical tests and procedures. Ensure everyday patients paying cash get the lowest discounted rate that the hospital gives to big insurance companies. Let what you pay to an out-of-network doctor count directly toward your yearly insurance deductible. Require insurance companies to approve common treatments within three days instead of letting paperwork delay your care.

chunks.title: Economy - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: “California passes heavy regulations. New York sends you the bill. Florida puts out the welcome mat. Bureaucratic delays shouldn't stop honest people from opening a business and earning a living.” Put every business, building, and road permit on an open state website with a ticking clock, forcing local offices to approve projects on time. Bring all major development permits under a single digital hub so job creators spend less time in lines and more time hiring workers. Route complicated business lawsuits through specialized judges so commercial fights don't clog up everyday neighborhood courtrooms.

chunks.title: Economy - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Keep our state personal income tax at zero, make sure Tallahassee balances its books responsibly every single year, and cut taxes at every opportunity.

chunks.title: Law and Order - Byron Donalds for Governor
chunks.text: Law and Order - Byron Donalds for Governor “We must secure our borders, keep local neighborhoods safe, stop taxpayer handouts to illegal immigration, and keep deadly drugs off our streets.” Cut off state funds, subsidies, and free perks that encourage illegal immigration into Florida. Require every Florida business to use the E-Verify system so legal workers keep the jobs and wages they've earned. Coordinate state and local police directly with federal authorities to quickly deport noncitizens who commit crimes in our communities. Target drug cartels with heavy penalties and joint police task forces to take deadly fentanyl off Florida streets.

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor Florida Was Built By People Who Arrived With Hope How we treat the people who come here says everything about who we are, and who we intend to be. David Jolly will fight for immigration reform that secures our borders while treating immigrants with dignity and creating a lawful pathway to legal status and work. He opposes state laws that punish working families and destabilize communities, supports keeping the promise to Dreamers who grew up here, and wants local police to focus on public safety rather than deportation enforcement. Florida's economy depends on immigrant labor in agriculture, construction, and healthcare.

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: Nearly one in four Floridians was born somewhere else, and they are our farmworkers, our nurses, our small business owners, and the family two doors down. When policy treats every immigrant as a threat, it doesn't just target strangers, it fractures the communities and the workforce that hold our state together. We can be a place that keeps its laws and its heart at the same time.

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: Florida did not become Florida by turning people away. The children of Operation Pedro Pan, the families of the Mariel boatlift, the Haitian, Venezuelan, Colombian, and Cuban communities that made Miami one of the great cities of the hemisphere, they are the proof of what welcome can build. That legacy is not a burden. It is our inheritance, and we should live up to it.

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: People want a system that is fair, predictable, and secure, and right now they don't have one. Families wait years for a hearing while the courts drown in a backlog no one seems willing to fix. I will fight for real reform that gives border security teeth and gives people a lawful, honest path, because a broken system helps no one and endangers everyone. Stop Punishing the People Who Feed and Build Florida

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: Immigrants make up a huge share of the hands in our fields, our construction sites, and our kitchens. Laws written to make headlines have left crops in the ground and projects stalled, and the cost lands on every Floridian at the grocery store and the closing table. We should be growing our economy, not chasing away the workers and the entrepreneurs who power it. Public safety matters, and so does telling the truth about it. When local police are turned into deportation agents, victims and witnesses stop coming forward, and everyone becomes less safe. I will stand with the officers and sheriffs who know that trust, not fear, is what keeps a community whole.

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: Tens of thousands of young Floridians were brought here as children and know no other home. They went to our schools, joined our workforce, and built their lives beside ours in good faith. Leaving them in permanent limbo is a failure of nerve and of decency, and it is long past time to give them the certainty they have earned. A Florida Big Enough for Everyone Who Loves It We can protect our borders, honor our laws, and still be the state that opens the door, because that is the Florida our own history demands of us. Q. Does David Jolly support border security?

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: Yes. Border security and compassionate immigration reform are both achievable when we start from shared values. The focus should be on federal border enforcement, not targeting immigrants who are already settled, working, and contributing to Florida communities. Q. What about DACA recipients in Florida? Florida has over 20,000 DACA recipients who were brought here as children, work legally, and pay taxes but face uncertain futures. They deserve a pathway to permanent legal status, which requires federal congressional action. Q. Why does Florida's economy depend on immigrants?

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: Nearly one in four Floridians is foreign-born, and immigrants make up over a quarter of the state workforce. They are essential in agriculture, construction, hospitality, and healthcare, and punitive state laws have already left crops unharvested and projects stalled, raising costs for everyone. Q. What is his position on state immigration enforcement laws? State laws that mandate E-Verify, criminalize transporting undocumented immigrants, and turn local police into deportation agents hurt Florida's workforce and make communities less safe. These laws cannot substitute for real federal reform and should be opposed. Q. Will this help Haitian and Venezuelan families in Florida?

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: Florida has the largest Haitian-American and Venezuelan-American populations in the U.S., and both communities face concerns about deportations and the end of humanitarian programs. Jolly's call for compassionate reform and a pathway to legal status and work is aimed at families who fled crisis but don't have access to the legal pathways Cuban-Americans have. Q. Why does he reference Miami's history with refugees? The Mariel boatlift brought 125,000 Cubans to Florida in 1980, and Operation Pedro Pan brought over 14,000 unaccompanied Cuban children in the early 1960s. Miami's prosperity today proves what Florida can build when we welcome immigrants instead of turning them away.

chunks.title: Immigration Reform: David Jolly for Florida Governor
chunks.text: Q. Does he support legal status for undocumented immigrants already here? Yes. Jolly supports a pathway to legal status and to work, particularly for long-term residents and those with U.S. citizen children. At the state level, his approach is to stop using state law to disrupt working families already contributing to Florida communities. Q. How does recent immigration enforcement affect Florida communities? Federal immigration arrests in Florida have surged dramatically, with over a third involving people with no criminal history. When people working and sending their kids to school are suddenly targeted, it disrupts families and communities that were thriving and safe.

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly Giving Florida's Families Access to Florida's Universities Hard work should be enough. Right now, for too many Florida students, it isn't. David Jolly believes qualified Florida students who work hard in Florida high schools should have preferred application status at Florida's public universities. He argues that Florida's universities should serve Florida families first, ensuring that in-state students are not losing seats to out-of-state applicants at schools built and funded by Florida taxpayers. This policy would prioritize access for students who grew up in Florida classrooms and want to build their futures in the state.

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: Florida's universities should work for Florida's families first. Across Florida, students are doing everything right. They're earning the grades. Putting in the hours. Following the path they've been told leads to opportunity. And then they're being turned away from their own state's flagship universities. Not because they aren't qualified. Because the system has stopped prioritizing them. This isn't an admissions policy. It's a broken promise. Florida is home to some of the nation's best colleges and universities. That's something to be proud of. But pride means nothing if Florida families can't access what belongs to them.

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: Right now, qualified students from this state are losing seats to out-of-state applicants. Students whose families have built Florida. Paid Florida taxes. Supported Florida schools. They're being told there isn't room. For some, this is called a fairness issue. For the families living it, it's something else. It's watching a child's future narrow because the state didn't put them first. It's the realization that working hard in Florida schools doesn't guarantee a shot at a Florida university. It means recognizing that access to higher education is not a luxury. It's the foundation of economic security, career opportunity, and the ability to stay in the state you call home.

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: It means understanding that when Florida's universities prioritize out-of-state enrollment for revenue, they're trading the futures of Florida families for a budget line. It means ensuring that qualified Florida students have preferred application status at Florida's public universities. Not as a favor. As policy. Floridians deserve a state that works for them. That starts with education. This isn't about closing doors to others. It's about opening them wider for the students who've earned their place here. Students who grew up in Florida classrooms. Who participated in Florida communities. Who want to build their lives in this state.

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: The question is not whether Florida's universities are excellent. The question is whether they serve the people of Florida first. Right now, they don't. And that can change. David Jolly believes that Florida families deserve priority at Florida's public universities. That a student who works hard in a Florida high school should have a real shot at a University of Florida or Florida State education. That the state's investment in higher education should benefit the state's students before anyone else.

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: This is about fairness. It's about making sure the system rewards effort, not zip codes outside state lines. It's about ensuring that a Florida degree is something Florida families can actually reach. Florida's universities should serve Florida's families. If you believe that, add your voice. Education is the promise that hard work leads somewhere. For Florida's students, that promise is slipping away. Not because they aren't trying. Because the system has stopped putting them first.

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: That ends when leadership changes. When policy reflects what families already know to be true. That if you grow up here, work hard here, and want to build your future here, Florida's universities should make room for you. This is what access looks like. And it's long overdue. Q. Is it really getting harder for my child to get into UF or FSU? Yes, both have become far more competitive. Florida State's admit rate dropped from about 55% in 2014 to 25% by 2023, and UF admitted only about 1 in 5 applicants for the Class of 2029. Many qualified Florida students who would have been admitted years ago are now turned away.

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. Could my child lose a spot at a Florida university to an out-of-state student? It can happen, which is exactly the concern. With admit rates around one in four or one in five at the flagships, and out-of-state students often paying much higher tuition, supporters argue that a qualified Florida student should not lose a subsidized seat to an applicant from another state. Q. Would giving Florida students preference hurt UF's national ranking?

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: There is little reason to think so. UF already draws nearly 92,000 applications with very strong students, and Florida's graduating classes are large and academically deep. UF has held a top public university spot for eight straight years, and prioritizing in-state students is what most leading public universities are designed to do. Q. Are Florida's universities actually good enough to fight for access? Yes, they are among the best public universities in the country. The University of Florida ranks No. 7 among public universities and No. 30 nationally, and Florida has held the No. 1 spot for higher education in state rankings since 2017. That excellence is exactly why access matters.

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. Can my child transfer to a Florida university from community college? Yes, and it is one of the most reliable paths. Under Florida's 2+2 system, a student who earns an Associate in Arts degree at a state college is guaranteed admission to finish a bachelor's degree at a state university, and transfer students already get priority over out-of-state applicants by law. Q. Does family background still determine whether kids go to college?

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: Strongly. About 66% of adults with at least one college-graduate parent earned a bachelor's degree themselves, compared with just 25% of adults whose parents did not finish college. A child's odds of completing a four-year degree are heavily shaped by whether their parents had one. Q. Do most college students actually graduate? Not as many as people assume. According to the National Center for Education Statistics, 63% of first-time, full-time students who start at a public four-year university earn a bachelor's degree at that same school within six years. That means more than a third do not finish on time at their starting institution. Q. How many public universities does Florida have?

chunks.title: Florida Universities Access for Florida Families – David Jolly
chunks.text: Florida has 12 public universities in its State University System, serving more than 430,000 students. Together these schools make up the second-largest public university system in the country and include the University of Florida, Florida State, the University of South Florida, the University of Central Florida, and Florida International among others. In depth David Jolly discusses FAMU at an event in Tallahassee

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision Florida has one of the largest economies in the world. The question is what we do with it. Florida's $1.7 trillion economy requires long-term vision focused on four pillars: making Florida a leading technology economy by investing in infrastructure and talent ecosystems that attract founders and engineers, renewing agriculture through sustainable practices and support for farmers, protecting and investing in tourism by maintaining infrastructure and workforce, and keeping Florida's top talent while attracting the world's best by building an economy where innovation and opportunity are real.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: An economy this size deserves leadership that thinks beyond the next election. Florida's economy is massive. One of the largest in the world. That didn't happen by accident. It happened because generations of Floridians built something real. But growth alone isn't enough. Not when the people driving that growth can't afford to stay. Not when short-term thinking replaces long-term vision. Not when politics gets in the way of progress.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: This is about what comes next. A technology economy that leads. An agriculture economy built for the next century. A tourism industry that remains the best in the world. And a state that keeps its best talent while welcoming the brightest minds from everywhere else. Different sectors. Different challenges. Same opportunity. Florida has the infrastructure. The talent. The universities. The geography. What it hasn't had is the political will to make technology a cornerstone of the state's economic future.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: That changes when leaders stop thinking in two-year cycles and start thinking in decades. When the state invests in the ecosystems that attract founders, engineers, and creators. When Florida becomes the place people move to build the future, not the place they leave because someone else offered a better path. This isn't about tax incentives alone. It's about creating an environment where innovation thrives. Where startups can scale. Where established companies want to headquarter. Where the next generation of technology is designed, built, and launched right here. Agriculture is Florida's foundation. It deserves a plan for tomorrow.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Florida's agriculture economy has fed this state and this country for generations. Citrus. Cattle. Sugarcane. Tomatoes. Strawberries. The land and the people who work it have been the backbone of Florida's economy long before the skyscrapers went up. But agriculture is facing pressures it hasn't seen before. Climate. Water. Labor. Market shifts. The question isn't whether those pressures are real. The question is whether Florida meets them with a vision or with politics.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: A renewed agriculture economy means investing in sustainable practices that protect the land for the next century. It means supporting the farmers and workers who make it possible. It means treating agriculture as critical infrastructure, not a talking point. This is Florida's heritage. It should also be Florida's future. Tourism built this state. It still matters. Tourism is one of Florida's greatest economic engines. Millions of jobs. Billions in revenue. Communities across the state that depend on it.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: The goal isn't to change that. The goal is to protect it. To make sure Florida remains the destination people dream about. To invest in the infrastructure, the workforce, and the environment that make tourism possible. That means clean beaches. Functioning airports. Roads that work. A hospitality industry that can hire and retain great people. And a state that understands tourism isn't just an industry. It's an identity. Florida is home to some of the brightest people in the country. Graduates from top universities. Entrepreneurs building companies. Researchers solving problems. Creators making culture.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Too many of them leave. Not because they don't love Florida. Because they don't see a future here that matches their ambition. That's a failure of leadership. Not of the people. Florida should be the state that keeps its top talent and attracts the world's best. That means building an economy where opportunity is real. Where innovation is supported. Where people who want to build something meaningful see Florida as the only place to do it. This isn't a recruitment pitch. It's a recognition that talent drives economies. And Florida has the foundation to compete with anyone. An economy this powerful deserves a vision this clear.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Florida's economy is one of the largest in the world. The question has never been whether it can grow. The question is whether it grows in a way that works for the people who live here. That takes leadership willing to think beyond the next cycle. Willing to invest in the long term. Willing to say that politics should never stand in the way of progress. This is Florida's moment. The economy is here. The talent is here. The opportunity is here. What's missing is the will to see it through.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Florida has the fourth largest economy of any U.S. state, with a gross domestic product of roughly $1.7 trillion, trailing only California, Texas, and New York. By most measures Florida's economy is larger than that of many countries. Q. Why do people say they can't afford to live in Florida if the economy is so strong? Because the cost of living has outrun what many Floridians earn. Median rent climbed nearly $500 a month between 2019 and 2023, and nearly 905,000 lower-income renter households are cost burdened. A truly strong economy is one where the people who keep it running can afford to live in the communities they serve. Q. Is Florida too dependent on tourism and real estate?

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Florida leans heavily on tourism and real estate, and that concentration is a long-term risk. Tourism supports 1.8 million jobs, and real estate is the single largest contributor to the state's GDP, but an economy weighted toward visitor spending and property is vulnerable. The smarter path is diversification: build a leading technology economy, renew agriculture, and expand trade and manufacturing. Q. Can Florida really become a technology economy?

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Florida already has the foundation to be a leading technology economy. NASA's Kennedy Space Center anchors a fast-growing aerospace hub that generates roughly 27,000 Florida jobs and more than $5 billion in economic output, with average salaries around $78,000. With the right investment in talent and innovation, Florida can attract more of the world's brightest minds rather than watching them build elsewhere. Q. How big is agriculture in Florida's economy?

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Agriculture is one of Florida's foundational industries, valued at about $300 billion according to the University of Florida. The opportunity now is to invest in a renewed agriculture economy that uses new technology, supports family farms, and helps growers weather hurricanes, foreign competition, and rising costs. Q. What role do small businesses play in Florida? Small businesses are the backbone of Florida's economy. They make up 99.8 percent of all Florida businesses and employ about 3.6 million people, roughly 41 percent of the state's workforce. In the most recent year of data, small businesses delivered about 65 percent of Florida's net new jobs.

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Q. Are wages keeping up with the cost of living? For many workers, wages are not fully keeping up with the cost of living. U.S. average hourly earnings rose about 3.4 percent over the year ending May 2026, while consumer prices rose 4.2 percent over a similar period. When prices outpace paychecks, real buying power slips, even though pay is technically going up. Q. How does Florida's economy compare to other states?

chunks.title: Strengthening Florida’s Economy: David Jolly’s Vision
chunks.text: Florida ranks fourth among all states with a gross product of roughly $1.7 trillion and grew 3.1 percent from 2024 to 2025. But Florida's real GDP per capita ranks 34th among the states, meaning the average economic output per person trails much of the nation. That gap between total size and individual prosperity is the heart of the challenge.

chunks.title: Insurance Proposal Facts: David Jolly
chunks.text: Floridians are paying the highest home insurance prices in America. The private insurance market has collapsed. It's time for a real solution to this major crisis. “Losing campaigns lie. What Byron is doing is using fear to try to stop progress, because he knows there's a coalition of voters across the state ready to elect a Democratic nominee.”

chunks.title: Insurance Proposal Facts: David Jolly
chunks.text: Byron Donalds is lying to scare people with invented numbers. Ads from Byron Donalds lie and claim Jolly's proposal creates a $1,000 “Hurricane Tax.” The two “sources” the ad gives are a study that does not review Jolly's proposal (which the ad misspells) and an opinion blog post. Confronted about the invented “hurricane tax” figure, Donalds pointed reporters to an unrelated, existing Florida law that allows Citizens Property Insurance to charge a “hurricane tax” of a few hundred dollars after a storm hits.

chunks.title: Insurance Proposal Facts: David Jolly
chunks.text: Byron Donalds thinks you should pay an extra $4,500 a year for insurance. A state catastrophic fund would lift the overwhelming cost burden of hurricane and wind coverage off of Floridians' backs, reducing the cost of property insurance by 60–70%, or around $4,500 in average yearly savings. Currently, a Floridian seeking property insurance with wind and hurricane coverage on a $300k home pays an average of $7,136 a year. Without having to pay for that coverage, the yearly bill would drop to just $2,557 a year, a whopping 64% savings. (Based on Insure.com's Florida home insurance calculator, comparing rates for $1,000 deductible plans with and without hurricane coverage.)

chunks.title: Insurance Proposal Facts: David Jolly
chunks.text: Byron Donalds has no plan to actually lower insurance costs. His sole idea is “transparency.” Transparency doesn't save you money; it just shows you why everything is so expensive. Remember, the insurance industry that has given Byron Donalds more than a million dollars in donations wants Floridians to spend more money on insurance, not less. Insurance special interests paying for Byron Donalds' campaign appear to include Slide Insurance Holdings Inc ($503,000), Florida Insurance Council (FIC) Political Committee ($231,000), United Group Underwriters Inc ($153,000), The Baldwin Insurance Group Holdings LLC ($115,000), Heritage Property & Casualty Insurance Company ($100,000).

chunks.title: Insurance Proposal Facts: David Jolly
chunks.text: Jolly's model to fix homeowners insurance, in plain English. Hurricane and wind risk can make up 60–70% of a homeowners insurance bill. So instead of forcing every Florida family to pay private insurers to take on that enormous risk: Florida creates one strong, state-backed hurricane fund. We build that fund to a financially sound level and buy backup insurance for catastrophic storms. We fund it by making insurance companies pay the taxes they currently avoid, along with other revenue sources that don't put the burden back on homeowners. Private insurers no longer have to price that hurricane risk into your policy, which has the potential to cut homeowners insurance costs by 60–70%.

chunks.title: Insurance Proposal Facts: David Jolly
chunks.text: This is a model that works. We know it works because Florida already created a catastrophic fund, and Republican legislatures have run it for thirty years. But right now, that fund only bails out insurance companies. We want it to cover actual Floridians.

chunks.title: Insurance Proposal Facts: David Jolly
chunks.text: This will lower costs for Floridians. It can be funded through a mix of forcing insurance companies to pay the taxes they currently avoid, a fee on real estate transactions, or existing tourist taxes. The fund can be rolled out responsibly, with coverage becoming available after a fiscally sound amount of money is set aside and backup reinsurance is in place. The Legislature will be involved in creating the specific policies, including the funding. In the end, the costs will be lower for Floridians, or we won't do it. Simple as that.

chunks.title: How Would David Jolly’s Catastrophe Fund Be Paid For?
chunks.text: How Would David Jolly’s Catastrophe Fund Be Paid For? How would David Jolly's catastrophe fund be paid for? It can be funded through a mix of forcing insurance companies to pay the taxes they avoid, a fee on real estate transactions, or existing tourist taxes. A mix of forcing insurance companies to pay the taxes they currently avoid, a fee on real estate transactions, or existing tourist taxes. The Legislature will be involved in creating the specific policies, including the funding. Coverage does not begin until a fiscally sound amount of money is set aside and backup reinsurance for catastrophic storms is in place.

chunks.title: How Would David Jolly’s Catastrophe Fund Be Paid For?
chunks.text: There is no annual charge on homeowners. There is no "$1,000 hurricane tax." The claim that there is comes from a Byron Donalds ad whose sources are a legislative feasibility study of a different proposal and an opinion blog post. Does David Jolly want a $1,000 hurricane tax? The order matters. Florida creates the fund. The fund is built to a financially sound level and buys reinsurance for catastrophic storms. Only then does coverage become available, and only then do private insurers stop pricing hurricane risk into policies. In the end, the costs will be lower for Floridians, or it does not happen. Will the catastrophe fund raise costs for Floridians?

chunks.title: How Would David Jolly’s Catastrophe Fund Be Paid For?
chunks.text: No. The plan funds it through insurance companies paying the taxes they currently avoid and through other sources that do not fall on homeowners. The campaign has named a fee on real estate transactions and existing tourist taxes, as part of a mix the Legislature would write into law. Q. Who decides the final funding formula? The Legislature. The campaign has said the Legislature will be involved in creating the specific policies, including the funding. Q. When does the fund start covering homes? After a fiscally sound amount of money is set aside and backup reinsurance is in place. Not before.

chunks.title: How Would David Jolly’s Catastrophe Fund Be Paid For?
chunks.text: The funding sources, the rollout order and the Legislature's role are from the Jolly campaign's published proposal and its September 2026 statement on the Donalds ads. The campaign's tourist tax proposal was reported by the Orlando Sentinel on September 6, 2026, and the three funding sources by the Miami Herald . chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly Does David Jolly want a $1,000 hurricane tax? No. There is no $1,000 tax, fee, or assessment on homeowners anywhere in the plan to lower insurance rates. The number comes from a Byron Donalds ad, and when reporters asked him where it came from, he could not say.

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: No. David Jolly's plan does not create a $1,000 hurricane tax. It creates a state-backed catastrophic fund that carries hurricane risk so homeowners insurance can fall by 60 to 70 percent, paid for by making insurance companies pay the taxes they currently avoid and by other revenue that does not put the burden on homeowners. The "$1,000 hurricane tax" is a line from a Byron Donalds ad. The ad's two "sources" are a legislative feasibility study of a totally different proposal, and an opinion blog post. Asked for the study behind the number, the Donalds campaign did not name one.

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: The Donalds ad, titled "Disaster," asks: "How much will David Jolly's hurricane tax cost Florida? According to a new study, a thousand dollars per Florida family every single year." On social media, Byron Donalds wrote that the plan "would create a $1000 hurricane tax on Florida families and bail out big insurance companies." The plan contains no such tax. It is a state catastrophic fund that takes hurricane and wind risk off private policies. The plan, in plain English.

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: The ad points to two things. The first is a Florida State University feasibility study prepared for the Legislature's Office of Program Policy Analysis and Government Accountability, its "Expanded Windstorm Coverage Feasibility Study." It is a study of expanding Citizens Property Insurance wind-only coverage to every home in Florida, an idea from a 2025 House bill. It does not review David Jolly's proposal, and no public copy of it contains a $1,000 figure. What the study is, and who paid for it.

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: The second is an opinion column by former State Senator Jeff Brandes. A Florida Politics news article, reporting on the ad, wrote that "the campaign does not name the study behind the $1,000" and that Brandes's column was the closest public source for the claim. Brandes's "hurricane tax" language does not describe anything in the plan; it describes something different: the post-storm assessments Citizens Property Insurance can already charge under existing Florida law.

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: Confronted about the figure, Donalds pointed reporters to an unrelated, existing Florida law, the Jolly campaign said in its statement on the ads. Under that law, after a bad storm, Citizens Property Insurance can charge its own policyholders a surcharge of up to 15 percent, and if a deficit remains it can charge an emergency assessment of up to 10 percent a year on most other property and casualty policies in the state, such as homeowners, renters, auto, and boat, "for as many years as necessary until the deficit is eliminated."

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: That is not David Jolly's plan. That is the system Florida has today, and it is the reason Jolly's proposal would build the fund to a financially sound level and buy backup reinsurance before it covers anyone. Will the catastrophe fund raise costs for Floridians? "It's all lies," Jolly told reporters on September 14. Jolly's proposal "does not include an additional $1,000 tax for homeowners. No governor is going to do that. What it does include is 60 to 70 percent reduction in people's homeowners insurance rates."

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: And on the ad itself: "Losing campaigns lie. What Byron is doing is using fear to try to stop progress, because he knows there's a coalition of voters across the state ready to elect a Democratic nominee." Byron Donalds is lying because he is losing. Q. Is there a $1,000 fee on homeowners in David Jolly's plan? No. The plan contains no fee, tax or assessment on homeowners. It is funded by making insurance companies pay the taxes they currently avoid and by other revenue that does not fall on homeowners. Q. Where does the $1,000 number come from?

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: From a Byron Donalds ad. The ad attributes it to "a new study," but the study it links is a Florida State University feasibility study of expanding Citizens wind-only coverage, prepared for the Legislature's research office, which does not review Jolly's proposal. Florida Politics reported that the campaign did not name the study behind the number when asked. Q. What did Byron Donalds point to when asked about the number? An existing Florida law that lets Citizens Property Insurance charge post-storm surcharges and emergency assessments, up to 10 percent a year on nearly every property and casualty policy in the state. That law is in force today; it is not part of Jolly's plan.

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. What does David Jolly's plan actually do? It creates a state-backed catastrophe fund to carry hurricane and wind risk, built to a sound level and backed by reinsurance before it covers anyone, so private homeowners premiums can fall 60 to 70 percent. The full plan is at /homeowners-insurance/.

chunks.title: $1,000 Hurricane Tax? Claim Checked: David Jolly
chunks.text: The ad's wording is as reported by The Floridian on September 9, 2026. The finding that the campaign did not name its study, and that the Brandes column was the closest public source, is from Florida Politics . The study's title, author and sponsor are from its Florida ExpertNet listing . Citizens' surcharge and emergency assessment limits are from Citizens Property Insurance . David Jolly's remarks are from Florida Phoenix and his September 14 video . This page was last reviewed on September 15, 2026 and is re-verified as the story develops.
